title: The PL/I Programming Language I: System/360, Free-Form Syntax & Unified Data (1957–1966)
summary: Part 1 of the PL/I Programming Language series: a relaxed, generalist-friendly 100-question journey from the late-1950s divide between scientific FORTRAN and business COBOL through IBM's five-billion-dollar System/360 gamble and the 1963 3x3 Committee that created PL/I. With zero assumed computer-science jargon, learners explore how PL/I shattered the 80-column punch-card cage with free-form block structure, banished reserved keywords, unified binary floating-point and exact penny-accurate decimal math, and pioneered pointers, asynchronous ON-condition error handling, multitasking, and compile-time macros—concluding at the 1966 high-water mark of universal-language optimism.
topic_prompt: Teach Part I of a two-part series on the programming language PL/I for an educated generalist with zero prior computer-science or programming jargon. Cover the historical and technical forces that gave rise to PL/I and its core architectural features across 10 conversational sections: (1) the late-1950s split between scientific computing (FORTRAN, SHARE user group, fast binary floating-point math on the IBM 7090) and business data processing (COBOL, GUIDE user group, character files and exact decimal currency on the IBM 1401/7080); (2) why binary floating-point rounding errors make bankers furious about missing pennies, and how hardware incompatibility forced companies to maintain two separate computing staffs; (3) IBM's $5 billion System/360 gamble (1964) to unify scientific and commercial hardware, and the 1963 SHARE/GUIDE 3x3 committee's rush to design 'NPL' (New Programming Language, renamed PL/I); (4) breaking free of 80-column punch-card cages with free-form stream syntax, ALGOL-inspired block structure ('PROCEDURE', 'BEGIN...END'), local variable scope, and recursion; (5) PL/I's radical 'no reserved keywords' rule (where 'IF IF = THEN THEN THEN = ELSE;' is legal code) and how context-sensitive parsing worked; (6) unifying numbers for rocket scientists and accountants under one roof via binary floating-point, 'FIXED DECIMAL' arithmetic, and COBOL-style 'PICTURE' formatting masks; (7) rich composite data: hierarchical record structures ('DECLARE 1 CUSTOMER...'), whole-array math, array cross-section slicing, 'VARYING' character strings, and bit strings; (8) memory management and the four storage classes ('STATIC', 'AUTOMATIC' stack allocation, 'CONTROLLED', and 'BASED' pointer variables that brought dynamic linked lists to business and scientific code); (9) runtime resilience through asynchronous 'ON' condition handling ('ON ZERODIVIDE', 'ON ENDFILE', 'ON OVERFLOW') and early 'TASK'/'EVENT' multitasking; and (10) the compile-time macro preprocessor ('%DECLARE', '%DO') and the high-water mark of 1966 optimism that PL/I would soon replace both FORTRAN and COBOL.

Clarified plain-English definitions on first appearance for low-level terms (processor scratchpad slots/registers, subroutines, operations research, 4-bit sign nibbles in packed decimal, raw memory dumps, and tape read parity/corruption errors) and balanced multiple-choice options and correct_index distributions (0, 1, 2, 3) across all 10 sections.

sections.title: 1. Two Worlds of Computing: Scientific FORTRAN vs. Commercial COBOL (1957–1962)
sections.summary: Step into a late-1950s corporate computing center to see why early electronic mainframes were split into two rival tribes. Learners first meet a compiler—a translator that turns human-readable instructions into hardware machine codes—and then compare the scientific tribe (aerospace and physics labs using FORTRAN and the SHARE user group on fast IBM 7090 machines) with the commercial tribe (banks and insurers using English-like COBOL and the GUIDE user group to process millions of customer text records on IBM 1401 and 7080 systems).

chunks.title: A Tale of Two Glass-Walled Rooms
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine walking through the headquarters of a giant aerospace manufacturer in 1960. Down one corridor sits a chilled, glass-walled room where trajectory physicists calculate rocket orbits on an **IBM 7090 mainframe**—a room-sized electronic computer. Down another hallway sits a second glass-walled room where payroll clerks and accountants print thirty thousand weekly paychecks and track warehouse parts on an **IBM 7080** and an **IBM 1401**.

To an outside visitor, both rooms look almost identical: spinning magnetic tape reels, flashing operator consoles, and trays of stiff paper punch cards. Yet if a physicist carried a stack of rocket-trajectory cards down the hall and fed them into the payroll computer, the machine would halt in utter confusion.

Why did a single corporation in 1960 need two completely separate breeds of computers, two separate programming languages, and two separate staffs who barely spoke the same technical dialect? The answer lies in how early computing split into two rival tribes: **scientific computing** and **business data processing**.

questions.prompt: What would happen in 1960 if an aerospace physicist tried to run an IBM 7090 rocket-trajectory card deck directly on the company's commercial IBM 7080 payroll mainframe?
choices: The payroll mainframe would halt or reject the deck because the two machines used incompatible hardware and languages.
The payroll mainframe would run the trajectory math at half speed while formatting the output as accounting ledgers.
The payroll mainframe would execute the rocket equations normally because all 1960 IBM models shared one instruction set.
The payroll mainframe would pause only until an operator flipped a console switch from commercial mode to scientific mode.
questions.explanation: In 1960, scientific mainframes (like the IBM 7090) and commercial mainframes (like the IBM 7080 and 1401) had fundamentally different internal designs and programming languages, so programs written for one could not run on the other.

questions.prompt: Which two distinct computing tribes coexisted inside large corporations and government agencies at the end of the 1950s?
choices: Analog differential-analyzer mechanics and digital relay-switchboard operators.
University pure-mathematics theorists and commercial desktop-calculator clerks.
Scientific computing specialists and commercial business data processing teams.
Military cryptography analysts and real-time telecommunications engineers.
questions.explanation: Late-1950s computing was sharply divided between scientific computing (engineering, physics, trajectory calculations) and business data processing (payroll, billing, inventory, and accounting).

chunks.title: What Is a Compiler?
chunks.content_markdown:
Before we meet those two tribes, we need to understand how human beings talk to a machine made of switches and wires. Down at the metal level, a computer's central processor only understands **machine code**: raw patterns of numbers that command basic hardware actions like "copy the value in memory cell 402 into scratchpad slot A."

In the early 1950s, programmers had to write out those numeric steps by hand—a slow, error-prone chore. By the late 1950s, pioneers invented **high-level programming languages** that let humans write instructions using familiar algebraic formulas or English words.

Of course, hardware switches still cannot read algebra or English directly. The bridge between human and hardware is a special translator program called a **compiler**. You feed your human-readable program—called **source code**—into the compiler, and the compiler translates the entire recipe into a fast, ready-to-run package of machine code tailored for that specific computer model.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of a compiler in computer programming?
choices: It schedules batch jobs so high-priority scientific runs execute before overnight accounting jobs.
It translates human-readable source code written in a high-level language into hardware-specific machine code.
It sorts paper punch cards into numerical sequence before they enter the mechanical reading hoppers.
It checks magnetic tape reels for physical wear and copies data onto fresh backup reels.
questions.explanation: A compiler is a translator program that takes high-level source code (written using algebra-like formulas or English phrases) and converts it into the low-level machine code instructions a specific processor can execute.

questions.prompt: Why could a computer processor in the late 1950s not execute high-level source code directly without a translation step?
choices: High-level source code used alphabetical characters that magnetic tape drives could not store.
High-level source code omitted arithmetic operators and relied on human operators to supply them.
High-level source code could only be stored on paper cards rather than in electronic memory.
Hardware processors only execute low-level numeric machine instructions wired into their circuitry.
questions.explanation: A processor's electronic circuits are wired to recognize and execute specific numeric machine-code instructions, so human-readable algebraic or English source code must first be translated by a compiler.

chunks.title: The Scientific Tribe: FORTRAN and SHARE
chunks.content_markdown:
The first tribe to embrace high-level compilers was **scientific computing**. Physicists, nuclear engineers, and aerodynamicists typically read a modest batch of measurement numbers into memory, performed millions of intense mathematical calculations—sines, cosines, square roots, and matrix equations—and printed out a short table of results.

In 1957, an IBM team led by John Backus released **FORTRAN** (short for *Formula Translation*). FORTRAN let scientists write compact algebraic statements that looked like textbook math:

`DIST = VEL * TIME + 0.5 * ACCEL * TIME ** 2`

Here `*` meant multiply and `**` meant raise to a power. Two years earlier, in 1955, scientific IBM customers had founded **SHARE**, the first influential computer user group. Through SHARE, aerospace labs, universities, and defense agencies pooled their reusable code recipes (**subroutines**), demanded faster math hardware on machines like the IBM 704, 709, and transistorized 7090, and fiercely defended FORTRAN's mathematical style.

questions.prompt: What kind of workload was a typical late-1950s FORTRAN program designed to handle?
choices: Reading a relatively small set of numeric inputs and performing millions of intensive mathematical calculations.
Scanning millions of customer street addresses to print monthly utility bills with minimal arithmetic.
Sorting large corporate personnel directories alphabetically by employee last name and department.
Updating thousands of bank checking balances from daily deposit slips and withdrawal records.
questions.explanation: Scientific computing workloads centered on heavy mathematical computation (trajectories, physics simulations, engineering equations) over relatively compact numeric datasets, which FORTRAN's formula-based syntax expressed naturally.

questions.prompt: What was SHARE, founded in 1955 by scientific IBM mainframe installations?
choices: A federal standards committee that restricted high-speed mainframes to defense contractors.
A time-rental brokerage that leased unused overnight computer hours to local retail stores.
A collaborative user group where scientific computing labs exchanged software routines and shaped IBM hardware priorities.
A joint university consortium that built open-source replacements for IBM magnetic tape drives.
questions.explanation: SHARE was the user organization formed in 1955 by scientific customers of large IBM mainframes (such as the 704, 709, and 7090) to share code libraries and influence IBM's scientific hardware and FORTRAN development.

chunks.title: The Commercial Tribe: COBOL and GUIDE
chunks.content_markdown:
Walk across the hall to the **business data processing** department, and the workload flipped completely upside down. A bank or insurance company rarely needed square roots or trigonometry. Instead, commercial mainframes read *millions* of customer records from magnetic tape, performed simple addition, subtraction, and percentage multiplication on each account, and printed endless stacks of invoices, tax forms, and checks.

To serve this world, a committee backed by the U.S. Department of Defense and heavily influenced by Grace Hopper's earlier work created **COBOL** (*Common Business-Oriented Language*) in 1959–1960. Rather than compact algebra, COBOL used verbose, self-documenting English sentences so corporate managers and auditors could read the logic:

`MULTIPLY HOURS-WORKED BY HOURLY-RATE GIVING GROSS-PAY.`

In 1956, commercial IBM customers formed their own user organization, **GUIDE**. While SHARE championed scientific number-crunching on the IBM 7090, GUIDE championed character-handling, file processing, and exact decimal accounting on machines like the IBM 7080 and the wildly popular **IBM 1401**.

questions.prompt: How did typical business data processing workloads in 1960 differ from scientific computing workloads?
choices: Business workloads solved differential calculus equations on tiny datasets with minimal file input or output.
Business workloads processed massive volumes of text and financial records using simple arithmetic per record.
Business workloads computed three-dimensional aerodynamic simulations before printing short summary tables.
Business workloads required high-precision trigonometric libraries rather than magnetic tape file storage.
questions.explanation: Commercial computing was input/output-heavy: it moved millions of customer records (names, addresses, account balances) through simple arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, tax percentages) and formatted printed reports.

questions.prompt: Why was COBOL designed around English-like sentences such as `ADD OVERTIME TO BASE-PAY GIVING TOTAL-PAY`?
choices: Early commercial compilers could not parse mathematical symbols like plus signs or equals signs on punch cards.
English sentences took up fewer punch cards than algebraic formulas, saving card stock in large banks.
Hardware processors on the IBM 1401 executed English verbs directly without needing a compiler step.
Designers wanted business programs to be readable and auditable by commercial managers and accountants.
questions.explanation: COBOL was intentionally verbose and English-like so business analysts, managers, and financial auditors could read and verify commercial program logic without needing training in algebraic notation.

chunks.title: When Two Tribes Start Stepping on Each Other's Toes
chunks.content_markdown:
As long as physicists stuck to rocket trajectories and accountants stuck to payroll, the wall between FORTRAN/SHARE and COBOL/GUIDE seemed natural. By 1962, however, that neat boundary was crumbling from both sides.

Scientific engineers increasingly needed to manage huge equipment inventories, format readable project reports, and sort alphanumeric part catalogs—tasks where FORTRAN was clumsy and painful. Meanwhile, commercial businesses were discovering **operations research** (using mathematical models to guide business decisions): airlines wanted linear-programming math to optimize flight schedules, and oil companies wanted statistical models to blend refinery crudes—tasks where COBOL's wordy arithmetic was agonizingly slow.

Yet neither language could comfortably do the other's job, and the underlying IBM machines could not even read the numbers the same way. In the next section, we will look inside the hardware to see why a simple ten-cent coin caused a war between binary floating-point scientists and decimal bankers.

questions.prompt: Why did the strict division between FORTRAN and COBOL become increasingly frustrating for organizations by 1962?
choices: Both FORTRAN and COBOL lost support for magnetic tape storage when transistorized mainframes arrived.
Commercial banks abandoned decimal currency calculations in favor of pure trigonometric modeling.
Scientists increasingly needed text-report and file handling, while businesses increasingly needed statistical and optimization math.
Aerospace laboratories stopped performing numerical calculations and switched entirely to payroll processing.
questions.explanation: Real-world problems began crossing the boundary: scientific labs needed commercial-style file sorting and formatted reports, while businesses needed scientific-style math for operations research and forecasting.

questions.prompt: Which pairing accurately matches each late-1950s computing tribe with its primary language, IBM user group, and flagship hardware?
choices: Scientific: COBOL, GUIDE, IBM 1401; Commercial: FORTRAN, SHARE, IBM 7090.
Scientific: FORTRAN, SHARE, IBM 7090; Commercial: COBOL, GUIDE, IBM 1401 and 7080.
Scientific: COBOL, SHARE, IBM 7080; Commercial: FORTRAN, GUIDE, IBM 7090.
Scientific: FORTRAN, GUIDE, IBM 1401; Commercial: COBOL, SHARE, IBM 7080.
questions.explanation: The scientific tribe rallied around FORTRAN, the SHARE user group, and binary machines like the IBM 7090, while the commercial tribe rallied around COBOL, the GUIDE user group, and decimal/character machines like the IBM 1401 and 7080.

sections.title: 2. Missing Pennies and Divided Machine Rooms: Binary Floating-Point vs. Decimal Currency
sections.summary: Unpack the everyday math and hardware reasons why scientists and accountants could not easily share a single computer or language around 1960. Just as $$\frac{1}{3}$$ becomes an endless repeating decimal ($$0.3333\ldots$$) in base 10, ordinary ten-cent coins ($$\frac{1}{10}$$ of a dollar) become endless repeating fractions in base-2 binary floating-point math, creating phantom penny discrepancies that infuriated bank auditors. Meanwhile, incompatible hardware designs forced big corporations to fund two separate machine rooms, two training pipelines, and two maintenance staffs.

chunks.title: The Case of the Vanishing Penny
chunks.content_markdown:
Suppose a corporate controller in 1961 asks a young FORTRAN programmer to test the scientific mainframe by adding up ten thousand customer deposits of ten cents each ($$0.10$$ dollars). Any schoolchild knows that $$10{,}000 \times 0.10$$ equals exactly $$1{,}000.00$$ dollars.

Yet when the scientific mainframe prints the total, the paper sheet reads $$999.99$$ dollars—or perhaps $$1{,}000.0002$$ dollars! To a rocket physicist calculating the thrust of a booster engine, an error of two ten-thousandths of a unit is utterly meaningless noise, smaller than a gust of wind on the launchpad.

To a bank auditor, however, a single missing or phantom penny is a five-alarm emergency. In accounting, every column of numbers must balance to the exact cent, and a discrepancy of one penny can trigger days of manual ledger hunting to rule out fraud or embezzlement. Why did the world's fastest scientific computer stumble over a simple dime?

questions.prompt: Why did a tiny fraction-of-a-cent discrepancy matter so much to a 1960s bank auditor when a rocket physicist could safely ignore it?
choices: Rocket physicists only used whole numbers and never calculated fractions or decimals in trajectory equations.
Financial accounting requires exact cent-for-cent ledger balance, whereas physical measurements always contain small tolerances.
Scientific mainframes automatically corrected their own rounding errors whenever numbers exceeded one million.
Commercial banking regulations required all interest calculations to be truncated to whole dollar amounts.
questions.explanation: Physical engineering measurements naturally have small tolerances, so tiny rounding residuals do not affect a rocket's path; in financial books, however, accounts must balance to the exact penny.

questions.prompt: What surprising result could occur when a 1960s scientific computer repeatedly added ten-cent ($$0.10$$) amounts thousands of times?
choices: The accumulated total could drift off by a fraction of a cent or a whole penny due to internal rounding.
The processor would halt with an arithmetic overflow error as soon as the sum reached one hundred dollars.
The compiler would automatically convert the dimes into whole integer cents before compiling the loop.
The calculation would run ten times slower than multiplying two large scientific numbers together.
questions.explanation: Because ten cents ($$0.10$$) cannot be stored exactly in standard base-2 binary fractions, adding it thousands of times caused tiny rounding errors to accumulate into visible penny discrepancies.

chunks.title: How Scientists Pack Giant and Tiny Numbers: Binary Floating-Point
chunks.content_markdown:
To understand where that penny went, let's look at how scientific computers store numbers. Physicists work with values spanning colossal ranges—from the distance between galaxies down to the mass of an electron. Writing out twenty-five zeros by hand is clumsy, so scientists use **scientific notation**, splitting a number into significant digits (the **mantissa** or significand) and a power-of-ten scale factor (the **exponent**), such as $$6.02 \times 10^{23}$$.

Scientific mainframes like the IBM 7090 built this same idea directly into base-2 (binary) hardware using **binary floating-point representation**. Inside each fixed 36-bit memory word, the machine used 1 bit for the plus/minus sign, 8 bits for the exponent (scaling by powers of $$2$$), and 27 bits for the binary mantissa.

Because the radix point "floats" according to the exponent, binary floating-point hardware can multiply or divide astronomical and microscopic numbers at blazing electronic speeds.

questions.prompt: What are the two main numerical parts that allow floating-point representation to handle both astronomical and microscopic values?
choices: A fixed whole-dollar integer field and a fixed two-digit fractional cent field.
An 80-column card sequence number and a 6-bit alphabetical character code.
A numerator integer and an explicit prime-factored denominator integer.
A set of significant digits (mantissa) and a scale factor (exponent) that shifts the radix point.
questions.explanation: Like scientific notation, floating-point representation stores a number's significant digits (the mantissa) alongside an exponent that scales the value by powers of the base, letting the radix point 'float.'

questions.prompt: Why did scientific mainframes like the IBM 7090 favor binary floating-point hardware?
choices: It allowed rapid multiplication and division across vast numeric ranges within fixed-size 36-bit memory words.
It guaranteed that every base-10 fraction like one-tenth could be stored with zero rounding error.
It stored variable-length customer names and street addresses more compactly than character machines.
It eliminated the need for electronic memory by storing numbers on mechanical decimal gear wheels.
questions.explanation: Binary floating-point packed a wide dynamic range of numbers into fixed 36-bit words and let electronic circuits perform scientific arithmetic at high speed.

chunks.title: Why One-Tenth Repeats Forever in Binary
chunks.content_markdown:
Why does binary floating-point botch a simple ten-cent dime? Think about ordinary base-10 decimals first. In base 10, the number $$10$$ factors into $$2 \times 5$$, so fractions like $$\frac{1}{2} = 0.5$$ and $$\frac{1}{5} = 0.2$$ stop cleanly. But try writing $$\frac{1}{3}$$ as a decimal: you get $$0.333333\ldots$$ repeating forever! If your calculator only holds six digits, $$\frac{1}{3}$$ gets chopped off to $$0.333333$$, and adding three of them gives $$0.999999$$ instead of $$1.000000$$.

Now switch to **base 2 (binary)**, where place values are halves ($$\frac{1}{2}$$), quarters ($$\frac{1}{4}$$), eighths ($$\frac{1}{8}$$), and sixteenths ($$\frac{1}{16}$$). Because $$2$$ is the only prime factor of the base, any fraction whose denominator has a factor of $$5$$—including one-tenth, $$\frac{1}{10}$$—*cannot stop cleanly in binary*! In base 2, $$\frac{1}{10}$$ is an infinite repeating fraction:

$$\frac{1}{10}_{\text{ten}} = 0.00011001100110011\ldots_{\text{two}}$$

Chopping that endless pattern to fit inside a 27-bit hardware mantissa creates a tiny **decimal rounding error** on every single dime.

questions.prompt: Why cannot the decimal fraction $$0.10$$ ($$\frac{1}{10}$$) be represented-exactly in finite base-2 binary floating-point?
choices: Because the number ten is an even integer, and binary mantissas can only represent odd denominators.
Because the denominator $$10$$ contains a prime factor of $$5$$, turning $$\frac{1}{10}$$ into an infinite repeating binary fraction.
Because 36-bit memory words reserve all 27 mantissa bits for whole integers greater than one.
Because binary floating-point exponents can only shift the radix point to the left, never to the right.
questions.explanation: Just as $$\frac{1}{3}$$ repeats forever in base 10 because $$3$$ does not divide $$10$$, $$\frac{1}{10}$$ repeats forever in base 2 ($$0.000110011\ldots_2$$) because its factor of $$5$$ cannot be built from finite powers of $$\frac{1}{2}$$.

questions.prompt: Which of the following fractions CAN be represented with complete exactness in a finite base-2 binary fraction?
choices: One-tenth ($$\frac{1}{10}$$), because ten is the base of the decimal system.
One-third ($$\frac{1}{3}$$), because three is an odd prime number.
Three-eighths ($$\frac{3}{8}$$), because the denominator $$8$$ is an exact power of two.
One-fifth ($$\frac{1}{5}$$), because five is half of ten.
questions.explanation: In base 2, fractional place values are $$\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{8}, \frac{1}{16}, \ldots$$, so any fraction whose denominator is a power of two—such as $$\frac{3}{8} = 0.011_2$$—terminates cleanly with zero rounding error.

chunks.title: How Business Machines Kept Every Penny: Variable-Length Decimal Memory
chunks.content_markdown:
To avoid binary rounding errors altogether, commercial computers like the **IBM 1401** and **IBM 7080** were built on a completely different hardware philosophy. Instead of packing numbers into fixed 36-bit binary floating-point words, these business machines stored data **character by character** in base-10 decimal form.

Each individual decimal digit (`0` through `9`) or letter (`A` through `Z`) occupied its own 6-bit character cell in memory (plus a check bit and a special marker bit called a *word mark* that showed where a field of any length began or ended). When an IBM 1401 added $$0.10$$ to $$0.10$$, its circuitry performed genuine base-10 digit-by-digit addition—just like a human clerk working with pencil and ledger paper.

There was zero binary conversion and zero repeating-fraction truncation. Ten thousand dimes added up to $$1{,}000.00$$ dollars every single time, and a street address of 23 characters sat right next to a 7-digit account balance without wasting memory.

questions.prompt: How did commercial computers like the IBM 1401 avoid the penny rounding errors of binary floating-point machines?
choices: They used 128-bit binary floating-point words so the repeating binary fraction remained hidden.
They rounded every arithmetic result after each step using a hardware random-number table.
They stored digits in base-10 character form and performed exact digit-by-digit decimal arithmetic in hardware.
They restricted all banking software to whole-dollar amounts and ignored fractional cents.
questions.explanation: Commercial machines like the IBM 1401 and 7080 represented numbers as base-10 decimal digits in character cells and executed hardware decimal arithmetic, preserving exact penny accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why was variable-length character memory on the IBM 1401 so well suited for commercial record processing?
choices: It compressed every customer name and street address into a single 36-bit binary floating-point word.
It required every numeric and text field to occupy exactly 80 characters to match a punch card.
It executed trigonometric matrix inversions ten times faster than the scientific IBM 7090.
It allowed text fields like names and addresses of varying lengths to sit compactly alongside exact decimal numbers.
questions.explanation: By using marker bits (word marks) to define field boundaries of any length, character-oriented commercial machines handled variable-length names, street addresses, and decimal currency fields smoothly.

chunks.title: The High Cost of Architectural Incompatibility
chunks.content_markdown:
By 1962, the consequences of this hardware split—known as **architectural incompatibility**—were giving both corporate executives and IBM itself a massive headache. Because scientific mainframes (fixed-word binary) and commercial mainframes (variable-field decimal character) differed down to their memory cells, peripheral cables, and instruction sets, a customer who needed both kinds of work had to lease two separate computer systems.

Worse still, inside IBM itself, the company was fragmenting into rival engineering fiefdoms. By 1961, IBM was designing and maintaining half a dozen incompatible product lines (the 1400 series, 7070/7080 series, 7090/7094 series, and 1620 series), each needing its own separate compilers, tape drives, field-service technicians, and sales manuals.

Something had to give. In Section 3, we will watch IBM bet the entire company on a revolutionary new computer family that merged scientific and commercial hardware—and sparked an urgent race to invent a single unified programming language.

questions.prompt: What did 'architectural incompatibility' mean for a large company that needed both scientific engineering and commercial accounting in 1962?
choices: The company had to lease separate computer models, maintain separate programming staffs, and manage incompatible peripherals.
The company could run COBOL and FORTRAN on the same processor, but only by rebooting between jobs.
The company had to convert all customer names into binary floating-point numbers before printing checks.
The company could share tape drives and compilers across all machines, but had to buy two different styles of punch cards.
questions.explanation: Because scientific and commercial machines had incompatible memory layouts, instruction sets, and languages, enterprises had to pay for duplicate hardware rooms, duplicate peripherals, and separate specialist teams.

questions.prompt: How did maintaining multiple incompatible computer lines affect IBM internally by the early 1960s?
choices: It lowered IBM's software costs because one compiler worked identically across all six product lines.
It splintered IBM's engineering and software budgets across half a dozen competing, non-interchangeable product families.
It allowed IBM to standardize on a single magnetic tape drive and card reader for every customer.
It convinced IBM executives to phase out commercial mainframes and focus strictly on aerospace labs.
questions.explanation: IBM's proliferation of incompatible product lines (1401, 7080, 7090, 1620, 7070) stretched its hardware engineers, compiler writers, and maintenance crews dangerously thin across separate ecosystems.

sections.title: 3. IBM's System/360 Gamble and the 3x3 Committee: From NPL to PL/I (1963–1964)
sections.summary: Follow IBM's historic five-billion-dollar bet on the System/360 (announced in April 1964), a single family of computers engineered to run both high-speed scientific math and penny-exact commercial record-keeping on the same hardware. To give this unified machine a unified voice, IBM and its SHARE and GUIDE user groups formed the six-person '3x3 Committee' in late 1963, working at breakneck speed in hotel rooms to design 'NPL' (New Programming Language)—soon renamed PL/I (Programming Language One) after the UK's National Physical Laboratory objected to the initials.

chunks.title: A Five-Billion-Dollar Bet on All 360 Degrees
chunks.content_markdown:
In April 1964, IBM Chairman Thomas J. Watson Jr. unveiled the boldest gamble in corporate history: the **IBM System/360**. Fortune magazine memorably dubbed it "IBM's five-billion-dollar gamble"—a price tag exceeding the wartime Manhattan Project and more than twice IBM's total annual revenue.

Why the name *360*? Like the $$360^\circ$$ of a complete compass circle, System/360 was engineered to cover every direction of computing—scientific, commercial, engineering, and real-time communications—within a single compatible family of mainframes.

For the first time, a single processor contained *both* high-speed binary floating-point circuitry for rocket scientists *and* exact hardware decimal arithmetic and 8-bit character bytes for bank accountants. Better still, a customer could start with a modest Model 30 and upgrade to a powerhouse Model 65 or Model 75 without rewriting existing machine-level programs. Hardware had finally been unified under one roof.

questions.prompt: Why did IBM name its revolutionary 1964 mainframe family the 'System/360'?
choices: Each processor used a 360-bit memory word to store ten 36-bit scientific numbers at once.
Like the 360 degrees of a full circle, one compatible hardware family served the entire spectrum of scientific and commercial computing.
The architecture combined the model numbers of the commercial IBM 1401 and scientific IBM 7090.
The system executed 360 thousand floating-point instructions per second on every model.
questions.explanation: The name '360' evoked the 360 degrees of a complete circle, signaling that a single compatible family of machines could handle every type of workload—both scientific and commercial.

questions.prompt: How did the IBM System/360 hardware resolve the numeric conflict between scientific physicists and commercial accountants?
choices: It built both high-speed binary floating-point circuits and exact decimal character arithmetic into the same processor architecture.
It replaced binary floating-point completely with 64-digit variable-length decimal arithmetic for all scientific programs.
It required customers to install two separate central processor cabinets connected by a shared magnetic tape drive.
It converted all commercial currency figures into 36-bit binary words and rounded results at the line printer.
questions.explanation: System/360 processors included instruction sets and hardware circuitry for both fast binary floating-point math and exact base-10 decimal and 8-bit character operations.

chunks.title: One Machine, Still Two Languages? Enter the 3x3 Committee
chunks.content_markdown:
Unifying the hardware solved only half the puzzle. Even on a shiny new System/360, if physicists kept writing in FORTRAN and accountants kept writing in COBOL, a company's programmers would still live in two separate worlds—and nobody could easily write a single program that combined complex scientific math with rich business file handling.

At first, IBM and the scientific **SHARE** user group hoped simply to stretch FORTRAN into a hypothetical "FORTRAN VI" by bolting on commercial text and decimal features. When they inspected FORTRAN's rigid 1950s skeleton, however, they realized that pasting business features onto FORTRAN was like welding a flatbed delivery truck onto a Formula One race car.

So in October 1963, IBM and SHARE formed the famous **Advanced Language Development Committee**—universally nicknamed the **3x3 Committee** because it paired **three IBM language designers** (led by George Radin and Bruce Rosenblatt) with **three SHARE customer representatives** (later joined by observers from the commercial **GUIDE** user group) to design a clean, unified successor from scratch.

questions.prompt: Why was the group chartered in October 1963 to design a unified programming language nicknamed the '3x3 Committee'?
choices: They were given exactly three months to merge three existing compilers into one software package.
They designed the language around three numeric types and three character string formats.
The core working group paired three representatives from IBM with three customer representatives from the SHARE user group.
They divided the language specification into three scientific chapters and three commercial chapters.
questions.explanation: The committee originally consisted of three IBM employees and three representatives from the SHARE user organization (with GUIDE representatives soon participating as well), earning it the shorthand '3x3 Committee.'

questions.prompt: What was the initial plan before the 3x3 Committee decided to design an entirely new programming language?
choices: To require all scientific programmers on the System/360 to write orbital equations in extended COBOL.
To translate all existing FORTRAN and COBOL programs directly into System/360 machine code without a high-level language.
To adopt European ALGOL 60 unchanged as the sole commercial and scientific language for System/360.
To expand FORTRAN into a 'FORTRAN VI' by adding commercial character and decimal capabilities.
questions.explanation: IBM and SHARE initially set out to define 'FORTRAN VI' with business and character extensions, but quickly concluded that FORTRAN's rigid card-column syntax could not cleanly support modern block structure and commercial data types.

chunks.title: Motel-Room Marathons and the Birth of 'NPL'
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine trying to design an ambitious, all-purpose programming language while the five-billion-dollar System/360 announcement date is hurtling toward you like an express train. Between October 1963 and February 1964, the 3x3 Committee worked at a breathless, almost frantic pace, holding marathon weekend sessions in New York and California hotel and motel rooms because IBM's secret System/360 labs were tightly compartmentalized.

Instead of favoring one tribe over the other, the committee drew inspiration from three sources at once:
1. From **FORTRAN**, they took compact algebraic formulas and fast scientific floating-point arrays.
2. From **COBOL**, they took hierarchical business records, exact decimal currency math, and report-formatting masks.
3. From **ALGOL 60**—an elegant European algorithmic language created in 1960—they took free-form layout and structured program blocks.

By March 1964, they presented their specification to SHARE under the working title **NPL**, short for **New Programming Language**.

questions.prompt: Which three existing programming languages provided the primary design pillars for the 3x3 Committee's new language?
choices: FORTRAN for scientific math, COBOL for business records and decimal data, and ALGOL 60 for block structure and free-form syntax.
FORTRAN for English business sentences, COBOL for recursion and block structure, and ALGOL 60 for decimal currency masks.
COMTRAN for scientific matrix algebra, FACT for floating-point hardware, and RPG for recursive block structure.
FLOW-MATIC for binary floating-point, LISP for 80-column card layouts, and AUTOCODER for block scoping.
questions.explanation: The 3x3 Committee synthesized the strengths of FORTRAN (scientific computation), COBOL (business data records, decimal arithmetic, and formatting), and ALGOL 60 (free-form stream syntax, block structure, and recursion).

questions.prompt: What did the initials 'NPL' stand for when the 3x3 Committee unveiled its first language report in early 1964?
choices: National Physics Language.
Numeric Processing Logic.
New Programming Language.
Networked Procedure Library.
questions.explanation: The 3x3 Committee initially named its creation 'NPL,' standing simply for 'New Programming Language.'

chunks.title: Why 'NPL' Became 'PL/I': A Polite Letter from England
chunks.content_markdown:
How did **NPL** become **PL/I**? The twist came from across the Atlantic Ocean. IBM assigned its major compiler development effort for the new language to its British laboratory in **Hursley, England**, near Winchester.

Wait a moment, said British scientists when they saw IBM brochures talking about "NPL." In the United Kingdom, the initials **NPL** already belonged to one of the country's most famous scientific institutions: the **National Physical Laboratory** in Teddington (where computing pioneer Alan Turing had designed the ACE computer after World War II!). Having IBM's flagship software share the exact initials of Britain's national standards lab was a recipe for endless confusion.

After briefly flirting with the name *MPPL* (*Multi-Purpose Programming Language*), IBM settled in late 1964 on **PL/I**—pronounced "P-L-one" and standing for **Programming Language One**, written with a Roman numeral `I` to match the grand, authoritative style of System/360.

questions.prompt: Why did IBM abandon the original name 'NPL' in late 1964 and rename the language 'PL/I'?
choices: The U.S. Department of Defense claimed exclusive military ownership of the acronym 'NPL.'
The initials 'NPL' were already famously used in the UK by the National Physical Laboratory, causing confusion near IBM's Hursley lab.
Commercial GUIDE members objected that 'NPL' sounded too similar to scientific 'FORTRAN.'
System/360 line printers lacked the slash character unless a Roman numeral followed it.
questions.explanation: Because IBM's Hursley laboratory in England was leading the compiler effort and 'NPL' already stood for Britain's renowned National Physical Laboratory, IBM changed the name to PL/I (Programming Language One).

questions.prompt: How is the name 'PL/I' properly pronounced and what does it stand for?
choices: Pronounced 'P-L-eye,' standing for 'Processor Logic Index.'
Pronounced 'pliable,' standing for 'Parallel Linear Interpreter.'
Pronounced 'P-L-slash-L,' standing for 'Procedural Language Level.'
Pronounced 'P-L-one,' standing for 'Programming Language One.'
questions.explanation: The 'I' in PL/I is the Roman numeral one: the name is pronounced 'P-L-one' and stands for 'Programming Language One.'

chunks.title: A Bold Promise: Freedom Without Intimidation
chunks.content_markdown:
Combining the best of FORTRAN, COBOL, and ALGOL into a single language sounds wonderful on paper, but it raised an immediate practical worry. If PL/I contained every tool a rocket scientist, an insurance actuary, and a systems programmer could ever want, wouldn't the manual be so thick that a beginner could never write a simple ten-line program?

To solve this, the 3x3 Committee established a core design philosophy called **modularity and default freedom**. A novice programmer should be able to learn just the small corner of PL/I needed for today's task—never even knowing that advanced features existed—while the compiler quietly supplied sensible **default settings** for everything left unsaid.

The very first place programmers felt this new freedom was right on the paper punch card itself. In Section 4, we will see how PL/I smashed the rigid 80-column card cage that had trapped FORTRAN and COBOL programmers for years.

questions.prompt: How did PL/I's designers intend to keep such a feature-rich universal language approachable for beginners?
choices: By letting programmers write only the subset they needed while the compiler automatically supplied sensible defaults for omitted details.
By splitting the compiler into three separate products that forbade mixing scientific and commercial features.
By requiring every variable and procedure to specify all twelve data and storage attributes explicitly.
By restricting novice programmers to fixed-column punch cards until they enabled free-form mode.
questions.explanation: PL/I's designers emphasized rich system defaults so a programmer could use a small, familiar subset of the language without having to specify or even know about advanced options.

questions.prompt: Where did IBM locate the primary software engineering laboratory responsible for building the flagship PL/I production compilers?
choices: Poughkeepsie, New York.
San Jose, California.
Hursley, England.
Böblingen, Germany.
questions.explanation: IBM assigned responsibility for the PL/I language and its flagship F-level compiler to the IBM United Kingdom Laboratory at Hursley House near Winchester, England.

sections.title: 4. Breaking the 80-Column Card Cage: Free-Form Syntax, Block Structure, and Recursion
sections.summary: See how PL/I liberated programmers from the rigid column rules of 80-column punch cards, where starting a FORTRAN instruction in column 6 instead of column 7 ruined a run. Inspired by the European language ALGOL 60, PL/I treated code as a continuous stream of text in which statements could span lines freely and ended with a simple semicolon (`;`). It also organized programs into nested, self-contained rooms (`PROCEDURE` and `BEGIN...END` blocks) with private local variables and allowed procedures to call themselves recursively.
introduced_terms: block structure and lexical scope (PROCEDURE and BEGIN...END)

chunks.title: The Tyranny of Column 7
chunks.content_markdown:
Picture a tired programmer in 1962 sitting at a noisy mechanical keypunch machine, typing a FORTRAN program onto stiff paper cards divided into **80 numbered vertical columns**. The programmer wants to type a simple calculation: `TOTAL = PRICE + TAX`. By accident, their finger hits the `T` of `TOTAL` in **column 6** instead of **column 7**.

Hours later, when the batch printout comes back from the computer room, the entire run has failed! Why? Because FORTRAN and COBOL were prisoners of **fixed-column punch-card layouts**. In FORTRAN, columns 1 to 5 were strictly reserved for statement numbers, column 6 was a special marker meaning "continue the previous card," columns 7 to 72 held the instruction, and columns 73 to 80 were ignored by the compiler as card-sorting sequence numbers.

Typing one character a single millimeter to the left turned the letter `T` into a continuation marker and wrecked the program.

questions.prompt: Why would a 1962 FORTRAN program fail if a programmer accidentally started typing a new instruction in column 6 instead of column 7 of a punch card?
choices: Column 6 was rigidly reserved as a continuation marker for the previous card, while normal statements had to start in column 7 or beyond.
Columns 1 through 6 were ignored as card-sorting sequence numbers, so the first letter of the variable name was dropped.
Column 6 was reserved exclusively for the letter `C` to mark the entire card as an explanatory comment.
The FORTRAN compiler treated any character in column 6 as a command to halt compilation immediately.
questions.explanation: FORTRAN used a rigid fixed-column card layout: columns 1–5 held statement labels, column 6 indicated that the card continued the preceding line, and executable statements had to sit in columns 7–72.

questions.prompt: What did a FORTRAN compiler do with characters punched into columns 73 through 80 at the far right edge of a standard 80-column card?
choices: It treated them as continuation markers linking the line to the next card in the deck.
It ignored them as optional card-deck sequence numbers used to re-sort dropped decks.
It compiled them as numeric precision attributes for the variables on that line.
It used them as statement label numbers for `GO TO` jumps within the subroutine.
questions.explanation: Columns 73–80 were reserved for sequence numbers (so a dropped deck of cards could be mechanically sorted back into order) and were completely ignored by the compiler as program logic.

chunks.title: Free-Form Stream Syntax and the Mighty Semicolon
chunks.content_markdown:
Looking toward a future of magnetic tapes, disk files, and interactive typewriter terminals, the 3x3 Committee asked a liberating question: *Why should a programming language care where the edge of a paper card is?*

Borrowing from Europe's ALGOL 60, PL/I introduced **free-form stream syntax** to mainstream IBM computing. To the PL/I compiler, your program is not a stack of rigid horizontal stripes; it is a single, continuous stream of characters—just like prose in a novel.

Instead of using the physical end of a card to finish an instruction, PL/I ends every statement with an explicit punctuation mark: the **semicolon (`;`)**. You can pack three short statements onto a single line:

`A = 1; B = 2; C = A + B;`

Or you can spread one long, complex statement across four lines, indenting freely with spaces to make the logic crystal-clear to human eyes. Even comments could float anywhere inside `/* ... */` markers!

questions.prompt: How does a PL/I compiler know where one instruction ends and the next instruction begins?
choices: Every statement must occupy one card and stop before column 72 unless column 6 is punched.
Every statement must begin in column 8 and end with a period (`.`) at the right margin.
Every statement ends with an explicit semicolon (`;`), regardless of line breaks or column positions.
Every statement is separated from the next by a mandatory blank line or comment card.
questions.explanation: In PL/I's free-form stream syntax, statements are terminated by a semicolon (`;`), allowing multiple statements on one line or a single statement spread across several lines.

questions.prompt: How are explanatory human notes (comments) written inside a PL/I program?
choices: By punching the letter `C` or an asterisk `*` strictly in column 1 of a dedicated comment card.
By prefixing the note with a percent sign (`%`) and ending it with a semicolon.
By placing the note exclusively inside columns 73 through 80 on any statement card.
By enclosing the note between `/*` and `*/` delimiters anywhere a blank space is allowed.
questions.explanation: PL/I introduced bracketed `/* ... */` comments that could be placed anywhere whitespace was permitted—a syntax later adopted by C, C++, Java, JavaScript, and CSS.

chunks.title: Building Rooms Within Rooms: Block Structure
chunks.content_markdown:
Free-form syntax didn't just make single statements prettier; it let programmers organize giant programs into clean, self-contained architectural rooms—an idea called **block structure**.

In early COBOL, all data variables had to be listed in one giant global catalog (`DATA DIVISION`) at the top of the program. If fifty programmers worked on a huge payroll system and two of them accidentally named a temporary counter `TEMP-COUNT`, they would silently overwrite each other's numbers!

PL/I solved this with two kinds of nestable blocks: **`PROCEDURE ... END;`** (a named subroutine you can call from elsewhere) and **`BEGIN ... END;`** (an inline block nested right inside a flow of steps). Using a `DECLARE` statement inside a block creates a private variable whose **lexical scope** (visibility) is locked inside that room. Once execution leaves the block, that private `TEMP_COUNT` never collides with a variable of the same name down the hall.

questions.prompt: What problem in large team projects did PL/I's block structure and local variable scope (`PROCEDURE` and `BEGIN...END`) solve?
choices: It allowed procedures to share a single global `DATA DIVISION` without needing `DECLARE` statements.
It prevented programmers working on different sections from accidentally overwriting each other's identically named local variables.
It ensured that every variable in the program retained its value permanently in `STATIC` memory.
It eliminated the need for semicolons inside nested subroutines and loop bodies.
questions.explanation: By scoping variables locally inside a `PROCEDURE` or `BEGIN...END` block, two programmers could each declare a local helper variable (like `I` or `TEMP`) without interfering with variables of the same name outside their block.

questions.prompt: In PL/I, what is the visibility rule (lexical scope) when an inner block sits nested inside an outer `PROCEDURE` block?
choices: The inner block can define its own private variables and can also see outer variables unless an inner variable reuses the same name.
The outer block can read all private variables created inside the inner block, while the inner block cannot see outer variables.
Variables declared in the outer block are invisible inside the inner block unless passed as explicit arguments.
Nesting one block inside another merges all variables from both blocks into a single global namespace.
questions.explanation: Following ALGOL 60's lexical scoping rules, an inner block in PL/I has private access to its own declared variables while also inheriting visibility of variables in enclosing outer blocks (unless shadowed by a local declaration of the same name).

chunks.title: A Procedure That Calls Itself: Recursion
chunks.content_markdown:
What happens if a `PROCEDURE` is midway through its job and calls *itself* to solve a smaller piece of the exact same puzzle? In computer science, a self-calling procedure is known as **recursion**.

Imagine calculating the total weight of a corporate shipping crate that contains smaller boxes, which in turn contain even smaller boxes. The cleanest recipe says: *To weigh a container, add the weight of its outer shell plus the weight of each container inside it (using this exact same recipe!), stopping when you reach a plain item.*

In 1960s FORTRAN and COBOL, recursion was **strictly illegal**! Why? Because FORTRAN gave each subroutine only one fixed slot in memory for its variables and return address; if a subroutine called itself, it would trample right over its own unfinished work. In PL/I, adding the keyword **`RECURSIVE`** (`CALC: PROCEDURE(N) RECURSIVE;`) instructed the compiler to create a fresh, independent workspace on a push-down stack every time the procedure called itself.

questions.prompt: Why could standard 1960s FORTRAN subroutines not call themselves recursively?
choices: FORTRAN syntax lacked a `CALL` statement and required all code to sit in a single main block.
FORTRAN subroutines could not accept numeric parameters or return computed values to a caller.
Each FORTRAN subroutine had only a single fixed memory area for its variables and return address, so a self-call would overwrite its own in-progress data.
Binary floating-point hardware registers reset to zero whenever a subroutine branched backward.
questions.explanation: Because standard FORTRAN allocated variables and return locations statically (one fixed box per subroutine), a recursive call would overwrite the caller's own active variables and return address.

questions.prompt: How does a PL/I programmer enable a procedure to call itself safely to solve nested, self-similar problems?
choices: By declaring all of the procedure's local variables with the `STATIC` storage class attribute.
By enclosing the procedure call inside an `ON OVERFLOW` exception handler block.
By prefixing the `CALL` statement with a percent sign (`%CALL`) to unroll it at compile time.
By marking the procedure header with the `RECURSIVE` option so each active call gets its own fresh workspace.
questions.explanation: Adding the `RECURSIVE` attribute to a `PROCEDURE` statement tells the PL/I compiler to allocate a fresh activation frame of local variables on each recursive invocation.

chunks.title: The Freedom of Modern Program Structure
chunks.content_markdown:
Step back for a moment and look at what PL/I accomplished in a single leap. A programmer moving from 1962 FORTRAN or COBOL into 1964 PL/I felt as if heavy iron chains had been unlocked:

- No more counting across punch-card columns to see if a statement started in column 7 or crossed column 72.
- No more terrified tiptoeing around one giant global variable list where a single duplicate name could corrupt an entire payroll run.
- Structured loops (`DO I = 1 TO 10; ... END;`) and clean `IF ... THEN ... ELSE` branches that nested naturally to any depth.

Yet when programmers opened the PL/I manual to look up the list of "forbidden reserved words" that they weren't allowed to use as variable names, they found a blank page! In Section 5, we will explore PL/I's wildest grammatical rule: a language with **zero reserved keywords**.

questions.prompt: Which combination of structural features did PL/I adapt from ALGOL 60 and bring into mainstream commercial and scientific computing?
choices: Fixed 80-column card margins, one global data division, and static-only subroutines.
Free-form semicolon-terminated stream syntax, nested `PROCEDURE`/`BEGIN` blocks with local scope, and `RECURSIVE` procedures.
Level-numbered hierarchical data records, `PICTURE` currency masks, and English-sentence arithmetic verbs.
Implicit `I`–`N` integer variable naming, column-6 continuation markers, and numeric statement labels.
questions.explanation: PL/I brought ALGOL 60's free-form stream syntax (with `;` terminators), nested lexical block structure (`PROCEDURE` and `BEGIN...END`), and recursion into industrial IBM mainframe programming.

questions.prompt: In PL/I, how are multiple statements grouped together so they execute as a single unit inside an `IF ... THEN` branch or a loop?
choices: By wrapping the statements between `DO;` and `END;` (or `BEGIN;` and `END;`).
By placing all of the grouped statements on a single punch card separated by commas.
By indenting the statements four spaces to the right without any closing keyword.
By ending only the final statement in the group with a period instead of a semicolon.
questions.explanation: Because PL/I is free-form and ignores line breaks and indentation, multiple statements are grouped into a compound block using `DO; ... END;` (or a `BEGIN; ... END;` block with its own local scope).

sections.title: 5. 'IF IF = THEN THEN...': No Reserved Keywords and Context-Sensitive Parsing
sections.summary: Explore one of PL/I's boldest and most surprising design choices: the complete elimination of reserved keywords. Because COBOL reserved hundreds of English words—and any future language update might suddenly outlaw a variable name a programmer had already used—PL/I decreed that words like `IF`, `THEN`, `ELSE`, and `DO` were never off-limits as variable names. Learners trace how a context-sensitive parser reads sentence structure to decode legal brain-teasers like `IF IF = THEN THEN THEN = ELSE;` cleanly.

chunks.title: The Hidden Trap of Hundreds of 'Forbidden Words'
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine writing a commercial COBOL program in 1962 to track warehouse shipments. Naturally, you decide to name one of your variables `REPORT`, `FINAL`, or `DETAIL`. You feed your card deck into the computer—and the compiler angrily rejects your program!

Why? Because most programming languages treat their command words as **reserved keywords**: off-limits vocabulary that only the language itself may use, never a programmer naming a variable (an **identifier**). By the early 1960s, COBOL had accumulated **more than 300 reserved English words**. A programmer practically needed a dictionary pinned to the wall just to avoid picking an outlawed variable name.

Since PL/I combined scientific, commercial, and systems programming into one language, its total vocabulary of command words, options, and attributes was even larger than COBOL's. If PL/I made all of those words off-limits, how could a beginner ever pick a safe variable name?

questions.prompt: In most programming languages, what is a 'reserved keyword'?
choices: A word with a built-in language meaning that programmers are forbidden from using as a variable or procedure name.
A variable name that has been declared `STATIC` so its memory slot remains reserved for the entire run.
A procedure name that can only be called by the operating system during hardware interrupt handling.
A shared data structure stored in a central `%INCLUDE` library that individual programmers cannot edit.
questions.explanation: A reserved keyword is a word claimed exclusively by the programming language's grammar (such as `IF` or `MOVE` in many languages), making it illegal for a programmer to use as a variable identifier.

questions.prompt: Why did COBOL's list of more than 300 reserved words frustrate everyday programmers in the early 1960s?
choices: COBOL required every program to declare all 300 reserved words in its `DATA DIVISION` header.
Programmers constantly had to check a long list of forbidden words to avoid naming a variable after an obscure language keyword.
Reserved words could only be punched in columns 1 through 6, whereas variable names started in column 7.
COBOL compilers charged extra processing time whenever a program used more than twenty reserved words.
questions.explanation: Because COBOL reserved hundreds of everyday English business nouns and verbs, programmers frequently triggered compiler errors by accidentally choosing a reserved word as a variable name—even for features they never used.

chunks.title: Protecting Tomorrow's Programs: Forward Compatibility
chunks.content_markdown:
There was an even deeper problem with reserved keywords—one that haunted corporate managers who expected their programs to run for ten or twenty years. Suppose a bank writes a working program in 1965 and names a variable `TASK` or `DEFAULT`. Five years later, in 1970, the language committee releases an updated compiler that adds a brand-new feature using the keyword `TASK`.

If keywords are reserved, the bank's working 1965 program **suddenly breaks** the day the new 1970 compiler is installed, simply because an old variable name collided with a newly invented command word!

To prevent both problems at once, PL/I's designers made a radical declaration: **PL/I has zero reserved keywords.** Every single word in the PL/I language—even `DECLARE`, `IF`, `THEN`, `ELSE`, and `DO`—remains an **unreserved identifier** that a programmer may legally use as a variable name, guaranteeing strict **forward compatibility** as new keywords are added in future decades.

questions.prompt: How does banishing reserved keywords provide a 'forward-compatibility guarantee' when a programming language evolves over time?
choices: Programs written for an older mainframe model will run without recompilation on incompatible processor architectures.
Variables declared without precision attributes will automatically double their digit capacity in newer compilers.
Adding new keywords to a future version of the language will never outlaw variable names already used in existing working programs.
Compilers can automatically translate legacy FORTRAN and COBOL decks into PL/I without human intervention.
questions.explanation: When keywords are not reserved, introducing new language keywords in future compiler releases never invalidates existing user programs that happened to use those words as variable names.

questions.prompt: How many reserved keywords does the standard PL/I language have?
choices: Exactly eight—only the core control words `IF`, `THEN`, `ELSE`, `DO`, `END`, `CALL`, `GOTO`, and `RETURN`.
Exactly forty-eight—matching the forty-eight characters of the scientific keypunch character set.
More than three hundred—combining the core command words of FORTRAN, COBOL, and ALGOL 60.
Exactly zero—every keyword in PL/I can also be used as a programmer-defined variable name.
questions.explanation: PL/I has zero reserved keywords: any word in the language, including `IF`, `THEN`, `ELSE`, `DO`, and `DECLARE`, may legally serve as a variable name.

chunks.title: Decoding the Brain-Teaser: `IF IF = THEN THEN THEN = ELSE;`
chunks.content_markdown:
Wait a second—if no words are reserved, how can a compiler possibly tell whether a word is a command or a variable? It uses **context-sensitive parsing**: just as you understand the English sentence *"Police police police"* (meaning law-enforcement officers supervise other officers) by looking at where each word sits in the sentence structure, the PL/I compiler looks at grammatical position.

Suppose a mischievous programmer declares three numeric variables named `IF`, `THEN`, and `ELSE`, and writes:

`IF IF = THEN THEN THEN = ELSE;`

Let's walk through it left to right with the PL/I parser:
1. The first **`IF`** starts the statement, so it *must* be the conditional command keyword.
2. Next comes a condition: **`IF = THEN`**. Here `=` is a comparison test ("is equal to?"), so the second `IF` and first `THEN` *must* be variables being compared!
3. Right after the condition comes the second **`THEN`**, which in that slot *must* be the keyword introducing the action.
4. Finally comes the action: **`THEN = ELSE;`**. Here `=` is an assignment command ("store the value of variable `ELSE` into variable `THEN`").

questions.prompt: In the legal PL/I statement `IF IF = THEN THEN THEN = ELSE;`, what role do the second `IF` and the first `THEN` play?
choices: They are two variables whose stored values are being compared for equality inside the `IF` condition.
They are compound command keywords that start a nested conditional block inside the outer `IF`.
They are compile-time macro variables that the preprocessor strips out before compilation.
They are target labels for a conditional branch that jumps to the end of the procedure.
questions.explanation: After the opening `IF` keyword, the parser expects a boolean condition expression; in `IF = THEN`, the `=` is the equality comparison operator comparing the variable named `IF` with the variable named `THEN`.

questions.prompt: In the statement `IF IF = THEN THEN THEN = ELSE;`, why does the equals sign (`=`) appear twice with two different meanings?
choices: The first `=` assigns a value to `IF`, while the second `=` tests whether `THEN` and `ELSE` are equal.
The first `=` tests whether two values are equal in the condition, while the second `=` assigns a new value to a variable in the action.
The first `=` compares numeric values, while the second `=` concatenates character strings.
Both `=` signs perform value assignment, copying `ELSE` into `THEN` and then into `IF`.
questions.explanation: PL/I uses the same `=` symbol for both equality comparison (inside expressions like `IF A = B`) and value assignment (at the start of an assignment statement like `B = C;`), distinguishing them by grammatical context.

chunks.title: The Compiler Writer's Headache: Looking Ahead Around the Corner
chunks.content_markdown:
If context-sensitive parsing is so clever, why didn't every later programming language copy PL/I's "no reserved keywords" rule? Because while it makes life easy for the programmer, it gives the poor engineers writing the **compiler** a monumental headache!

Consider what happens when a PL/I compiler reads the start of this line:

`DECLARE (A, B, C) ...`

Is this a **declaration statement** creating three new variables named `A`, `B`, and `C`? Usually, yes! *Unless* the programmer previously created a three-dimensional array (a 3D grid of numbers) named `DECLARE` and is now writing an assignment statement:

`DECLARE (A, B, C) = 0;`

To know whether `DECLARE` is a keyword or an array variable, the compiler cannot decide on the first word; it has to **look ahead** past the closing parenthesis `)` to see whether the next character is an equals sign `=` or a data attribute like `FIXED`! That extra look-ahead machinery made PL/I compilers much larger and trickier to build than compilers for languages with reserved words.

questions.prompt: Why cannot a PL/I compiler immediately tell whether `DECLARE (A, B, C)` at the start of a statement is a variable declaration or an array assignment?
choices: Because PL/I allows array assignments to appear inside `DECLARE` statements without an equals sign.
Because parentheses in PL/I can denote either a list of procedure arguments or a comment block.
Because `DECLARE` could be the name of a user-defined 3D array if an `=` sign appears after the closing parenthesis.
Because all variable declarations in PL/I must be processed by the `%` macro preprocessor first.
questions.explanation: Since `DECLARE` is not a reserved word, `DECLARE(A, B, C) = 0;` is a legal assignment setting element `(A,B,C)` of an array named `DECLARE` to zero; the parser must look ahead past `)` to see if an `=` follows.

questions.prompt: What was the main engineering trade-off of PL/I's decision to eliminate all reserved keywords?
choices: It simplified the compiler's parser into a single pass, but forced programmers to memorize 300 forbidden words.
It sped up compile times on small mainframes, but prevented programmers from using short variable names.
It eliminated the need for semicolons at the end of statements, but required fixed punch-card columns.
It protected programmers from keyword collisions, but made the compiler's parser much more complex and memory-hungry.
questions.explanation: Unreserved keywords spared programmers from memorizing forbidden words and protected forward compatibility, at the cost of requiring complex multi-token look-ahead inside the PL/I compiler.

chunks.title: Abbreviations Without Fear
chunks.content_markdown:
Once the 3x3 Committee realized that context-sensitive parsing freed them from worrying about reserved-word collisions, they unlocked a delightful bonus for everyday programmers: **official keyword abbreviations**.

No one enjoys typing `DECLARE`, `PROCEDURE`, `DECIMAL`, `BINARY`, or `CHARACTER` hundreds of times on a stiff mechanical keyboard. In a language with reserved keywords, adding short abbreviations like `DCL`, `PROC`, `DEC`, `BIN`, and `CHAR` is dangerous, because short three- and four-letter words are the very names programmers love to pick for their own variables!

In PL/I, however, adding abbreviations was completely harmless. Whether you wrote the full formal statement:

`DECLARE TOTAL FIXED DECIMAL(7,2);`

or the brisk shorthand:

`DCL TOTAL FIXED DEC(7,2);`

the compiler understood both—and still let you name a variable `DEC` (perhaps for the month of December!) whenever you pleased. Speaking of `FIXED DECIMAL(7,2)`, how exactly did PL/I unify scientific and financial numbers? Let's find out in Section 6.

questions.prompt: Why could PL/I safely provide short built-in keyword abbreviations like `DCL` (for `DECLARE`), `PROC` (for `PROCEDURE`), and `DEC` (for `DECIMAL`)?
choices: Because keywords are not reserved, so a programmer could still use `DEC` as a variable name without conflict.
Because PL/I required all user-defined variable names to be at least six characters long.
Because abbreviated keywords were expanded by the keypunch machine before cards reached the compiler.
Because `DCL`, `PROC`, and `DEC` were only valid when preceded by a `%` preprocessor symbol.
questions.explanation: In a reserved-word language, reserving short words like `DEC` or `CHAR` would steal common variable names from users; in PL/I, context-sensitive parsing allowed both official abbreviations and variables named `DEC`.

questions.prompt: Which pair of PL/I statements is treated as completely identical by the PL/I compiler?
choices: `DECLARE X FLOAT BINARY;` and `DECLARE X FIXED BINARY;`
`DECLARE X FLOAT BINARY;` and `DCL X FLOAT BIN;`
`PROCEDURE MAIN;` and `BEGIN MAIN;`
`IF A = B THEN C = D;` and `ON A = B C = D;`
questions.explanation: `DCL` is PL/I's official abbreviation for `DECLARE`, and `BIN` is the official abbreviation for `BINARY`, so both statements declare `X` with identical numeric attributes.

sections.title: 6. Numbers for Rocket Scientists and Accountants: FLOAT BINARY, FIXED DECIMAL, and PICTURE
sections.summary: Discover how PL/I brought scientific and financial math under one roof by letting programmers choose exact numeric attributes in a `DECLARE` statement. An orbital physicist could request `FLOAT BINARY` for rapid scientific notation across huge ranges, while a payroll clerk in the very next line could specify `FIXED DECIMAL(7,2)` for exact dollars-and-cents arithmetic with zero binary rounding drift, or apply a COBOL-style `PICTURE 'Z,ZZ9V.99'` mask to format numbers automatically with commas, decimal points, and suppressed leading zeros.
introduced_terms: numeric data attributes (BASE, SCALE, MODE, and PRECISION)

chunks.title: One Program, Two Kinds of Math
chunks.content_markdown:
Suppose an electric utility company in 1965 is building a single master program on its new IBM System/360. In the first half of the program, engineers calculate high-voltage alternating-current power losses across hundreds of miles of transmission lines—work that cries out for fast scientific floating-point numbers. In the second half of the *exact same program*, the billing logic multiplies each household's kilowatt-hours by a tariff rate to print monthly electric bills—work that demands penny-exact decimal currency.

In 1960, those two jobs required two different languages and often two different computers. In PL/I, both calculations can sit side by side inside the same `PROCEDURE`.

Instead of forcing one rigid numeric representation on everyone, PL/I let programmers describe *how* each number should behave using a rich menu of **numeric data attributes** inside a `DECLARE` statement.

questions.prompt: Why would a 1965 electric utility company benefit from PL/I's unified numeric system?
choices: A single PL/I program could run both floating-point power-grid physics and penny-exact decimal customer billing.
A single PL/I program could convert all customer billing ledgers into approximate binary floating-point fractions.
PL/I eliminated the need to declare numeric types by storing all numbers as 80-character text strings.
PL/I restricted utility companies to whole-dollar integer math so fractional kilowatt-hours were ignored.
questions.explanation: PL/I let engineers use fast binary floating-point for physical grid modeling and exact fixed-point decimal arithmetic for customer billing within the very same program.

questions.prompt: How does a PL/I programmer specify whether a variable should behave like a scientific number or a financial currency number?
choices: By placing scientific variables in a separate `DATA DIVISION` file outside the main procedure.
By attaching explicit numeric data attributes to the variable in a `DECLARE` statement.
By writing scientific variable names in uppercase letters and financial names in lowercase.
By starting all financial statements in column 7 and all scientific statements in column 12.
questions.explanation: In PL/I, the `DECLARE` (`DCL`) statement assigns explicit data attributes (such as `FLOAT BINARY` or `FIXED DECIMAL`) to each variable.

chunks.title: The Four Dials of a PL/I Number: Base, Scale, Mode, and Precision
chunks.content_markdown:
When you declare a number in PL/I, you can adjust four independent dials—known as its **numeric data attributes**:

1. **BASE (`BINARY` or `DECIMAL`)**: Should the computer store the value in base-2 binary bits or base-10 decimal digits?
2. **SCALE (`FLOAT` or `FIXED`)**: Should the radix point float across huge scientific ranges (`FLOAT`), or stay locked at a fixed number of fractional places (`FIXED`)?
3. **MODE (`REAL` or `COMPLEX`)**: Is it an ordinary single number (`REAL`), or a two-part complex number with an imaginary $$\sqrt{-1}$$ component (`COMPLEX`) used in electrical and quantum engineering?
4. **PRECISION (`(p)` or `(p,q)`)**: How many total significant digits or bits $$p$$ should it hold, and (for `FIXED` numbers) how many of those digits $$q$$ sit to the right of the radix point?

Thus, a rocket physicist writes `DCL VELOCITY FLOAT BINARY(27);`, while an electrical engineer analyzing alternating-current impedance can even write `DCL IMPEDANCE FLOAT BINARY COMPLEX;`!

questions.prompt: Which four independent numeric data attributes can a programmer choose when declaring an arithmetic variable in PL/I?
choices: Length (`SHORT`/`LONG`), Sign (`SIGNED`/`UNSIGNED`), Alignment (`BYTE`/`WORD`), and Scope (`LOCAL`/`GLOBAL`).
Format (`CARD`/`TAPE`), Radix (`OCTAL`/`HEX`), Rounding (`UP`/`DOWN`), and Bounds (`MIN`/`MAX`).
Base (`BINARY`/`DECIMAL`), Scale (`FLOAT`/`FIXED`), Mode (`REAL`/`COMPLEX`), and Precision (`(p)` or `(p,q)`).
Storage (`STATIC`/`BASED`), Class (`TEXT`/`NUMERIC`), Level (`1`/`2`), and Mask (`Z`/`9`).
questions.explanation: Every arithmetic variable in PL/I is characterized by four orthogonal attributes: Base (binary vs. decimal), Scale (floating-point vs. fixed-point), Mode (real vs. complex), and Precision (total digits/bits and fractional digits/bits).

questions.prompt: Why did PL/I include a `COMPLEX` mode attribute alongside `REAL`?
choices: To group mixed customer fields such as names, street addresses, and balances into a single record.
To link multiple procedures together when a program was too large to fit in 64 kilobytes of memory.
To format multi-column financial balance sheets with automatic debit and credit symbols.
To support engineering and physics calculations that use complex numbers with real and imaginary components.
questions.explanation: `COMPLEX` mode let scientists and electrical engineers perform arithmetic directly on complex numbers (of the form $$a + bi$$, where $$i = \sqrt{-1}$$) without having to split real and imaginary parts manually.

chunks.title: The Accountant's Best Friend: `FIXED DECIMAL(p,q)`
chunks.content_markdown:
Now let's see how PL/I rescues the bank auditor from the missing-penny nightmare of Section 2. Suppose an accountant writes:

`DECLARE BALANCE FIXED DECIMAL(7,2);`

What does `FIXED DECIMAL(7,2)` command the System/360 hardware to do?
- **`DECIMAL`** tells the processor to store the number in true base-10 decimal digits (using System/360's built-in *packed decimal* hardware, which packs two base-10 digits into each 8-bit byte, plus a 4-bit half-byte at the end for the plus or minus sign).
- **`FIXED`** locks the decimal point in place rather than letting it float.
- **`(7,2)`** specifies the precision: store **7 total decimal digits**, with **2 of those digits strictly after the decimal point** (leaving 5 digits before the decimal point, covering values from `-99999.99` to `+99999.99`).

When you add `0.10` ten thousand times into `BALANCE`, the System/360 executes exact base-10 decimal hardware instructions. Not a single binary fraction is ever used, and the sum is `1000.00` to the exact penny!

questions.prompt: In the PL/I declaration `DECLARE PRICE FIXED DECIMAL(5,2);`, what do the precision numbers `(5,2)` mean?
choices: The variable holds 5 total decimal digits, with 2 of those digits located to the right of the decimal point.
The variable holds 5 digits to the left of the decimal point and 2 digits to the right, for 7 digits total.
The variable stores numbers in base 5 using 2 bytes of magnetic-core memory.
The variable reserves 5 array elements, each initialized to a starting value of 2.
questions.explanation: In PL/I `FIXED DECIMAL(p,q)`, the first number `p` is the total number of decimal digits stored (here 5), and the second number `q` is the scale factor—how many of those `p` digits sit after the decimal point (here 2, leaving 3 integer digits: `999.99`).

questions.prompt: Why does `FIXED DECIMAL(7,2)` completely avoid the penny-rounding drift seen in `FLOAT BINARY`?
choices: It uses 64-bit binary mantissas so base-2 rounding errors stay smaller than one-millionth of a cent.
It stores exact base-10 digits and uses the processor's decimal arithmetic circuitry rather than base-2 approximations.
It converts all fractional amounts into whole integers by multiplying every input card by one thousand.
It defers all addition until the end of the program and prints the raw unadded numbers on paper.
questions.explanation: `FIXED DECIMAL` stores numbers in base 10 (packed decimal on System/360) and performs true base-10 arithmetic, so decimal fractions like $$0.10$$ are represented with complete exactness.

chunks.title: Dressing Numbers for the Printer: `PICTURE` Formatting Masks
chunks.content_markdown:
