Keeping numbers exact inside memory is essential, but business computing has a second demand: when you print thirty thousand paychecks or utility bills, nobody wants to see raw computer numbers like `00042.50`. Customers expect human-friendly formatting with commas, decimal points, suppressed leading zeros (`   42.50`), or debit/credit signs (`CR`).

Borrowed straight from COBOL, PL/I's **`PICTURE`** attribute (abbreviated **`PIC`**) lets you define a character-by-character formatting mask right in your variable declaration:

`DECLARE NET_PAY PICTURE 'ZZ,ZZ9V.99';`

Here each character in the mask acts like a tiny stencil:
- **`9`** means "always print a digit here (even if it is `0`)."
- **`Z`** means "print the digit, or replace a leading `0` with a blank space."
- **`V`** marks where the internal algebraic decimal point lives for math.
- **`,` and `.`** insert an actual comma and decimal point into the printed characters!

Remarkably, PL/I lets you do *both* arithmetic (`NET_PAY = GROSS - TAX;`) and instant formatted printing on a `PICTURE` variable.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the `Z` character inside a PL/I `PICTURE` mask such as `PICTURE 'ZZ,ZZ9V.99'`?
choices: It forces the variable to reset to zero whenever an arithmetic overflow occurs.
It marks the position where the algebraic decimal point sits for internal scaling.
It suppresses leading zeros by replacing them with blank spaces so `00042.50` prints as `   42.50`.
It truncates fractional cents so only whole-dollar digits are printed on checks.
questions.explanation: In a `PICTURE` specification, `Z` stands for 'zero suppression': if a leading digit position holds zero, it is replaced by a blank space (and any comma to its left is also suppressed).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `V` and `.` inside the PL/I mask `PICTURE 'ZZ,ZZ9V.99'`?
choices: `V` suppresses trailing zeros after the decimal point, while `.` suppresses leading zeros before it.
`V` converts the number to binary floating-point, while `.` keeps the number in fixed decimal.
Both characters insert literal period characters, producing a double decimal point on the page.
`V` marks the logical decimal point for arithmetic scaling, while `.` inserts a literal printed period.
questions.explanation: `V` indicates the logical position of the decimal point for arithmetic alignment without taking up a character slot, whereas `.` is an insertion character that places an actual visible period into the formatted string.

chunks.title: A Clever Bridge (and a Subtle Surprise) in PL/I Defaults
chunks.content_markdown:
What happens if a programmer doesn't bother typing `FIXED DECIMAL` or `FLOAT BINARY`—or doesn't even write a `DECLARE` statement for a variable at all?

To make migrating FORTRAN programmers feel right at home, the 3x3 Committee kept a famous FORTRAN shortcut called **implicit typing by first letter**:
- Any undeclared variable whose name begins with the letters **`I` through `N`** (the first two letters of the word *IN*teger, such as `INDEX`, `J_LOOP`, or `MAX_COUNT`) defaults automatically to a whole-number binary integer: **`FIXED BINARY(15,0)`**.
- Any undeclared variable starting with any other letter (**`A`–`H`** or **`O`–`Z`**, such as `TOTAL` or `VELOCITY`) defaults to **`FLOAT DECIMAL(6)`**.

Notice the subtle twist: if you write `DECLARE AMOUNT FIXED;` and mention `FIXED` *without* specifying `BINARY` or `DECIMAL` or a precision, PL/I's partial-attribute default rules give you **`FIXED DECIMAL(5,0)`**—an integer with **zero fractional places** that silently drops your pennies! Next, in Section 7, we'll see how PL/I grouped individual numbers and text into rich structures and arrays.

questions.prompt: If a PL/I programmer uses two variables named `ITEM_COUNT` and `TOTAL_COST` without declaring either one, what default types does PL/I assign?
choices: `ITEM_COUNT` defaults to `FIXED BINARY` integer, while `TOTAL_COST` defaults to `FLOAT DECIMAL`.
Both variables default to 80-character text strings matching standard punch-card width.
`ITEM_COUNT` defaults to `FLOAT BINARY`, while `TOTAL_COST` defaults to `FIXED DECIMAL(7,2)`.
The compiler rejects the program because PL/I requires an explicit `DECLARE` for every variable.
questions.explanation: Inherited from FORTRAN's `I`–`N` integer convention, undeclared PL/I variables starting with letters `I` through `N` default to `FIXED BINARY(15,0)` integers, while those starting with `A`–`H` or `O`–`Z` default to `FLOAT DECIMAL(6)`.

questions.prompt: What subtle surprise awaits a programmer who writes `DECLARE AMOUNT FIXED;` in PL/I without specifying `DECIMAL`, `BINARY`, or a precision?
choices: PL/I locks the variable as a read-only constant whose value can never be changed.
PL/I supplies the default attributes `FIXED DECIMAL(5,0)`, which has zero fractional places and truncates cents.
PL/I assigns `FLOAT BINARY(53)` instead, reintroducing binary floating-point rounding errors.
PL/I treats `FIXED` as a variable name rather than an attribute and ignores `AMOUNT`.
questions.explanation: In PL/I, specifying `FIXED` alone defaults the base to `DECIMAL` and the precision to `(5,0)`—meaning five integer digits and zero fractional digits, so any cents assigned to `AMOUNT` are truncated.

sections.title: 7. Rich Composite Data: Hierarchical Structures, Array Cross-Sections, and Varying Strings
sections.summary: Tour the rich data containers that emerged when PL/I merged business record layouts with scientific matrix math. From COBOL came numbered hierarchical structures (`DECLARE 1 CUSTOMER, 2 NAME, 3 FIRST, 3 LAST...`) that grouped mixed customer fields into a single logical folder; from scientific computing came whole-array arithmetic (`A = B + C;`) and asterisk cross-section slicing (`TABLE(*, 3)`) that pulled an entire column out of a grid in one stroke—joined by flexible `VARYING` text strings and compact bit strings.
introduced_terms: whole-array expressions and asterisk cross-section slicing

chunks.title: Grids of Numbers vs. Folders of Mixed Information
chunks.content_markdown:
Single numbers are useful, but real-world computing organizes data into larger containers. Once again, the scientific and commercial tribes of 1960 used completely different containers.

Scientists loved **arrays** (grids or tables where every box holds the *exact same kind of number*, such as a $$100 \times 100$$ grid of wind-tunnel air pressures). FORTRAN handled numeric arrays well, but if you wanted to bundle together items of *different* types—say, a customer's text name, integer birth year, and decimal account balance—FORTRAN had no clean way to group them.

Business programmers in COBOL had the exact opposite strength: they organized mixed customer data into **records** (like a paper folder holding a name slip, an address card, and a ledger sheet), while array matrix math in COBOL was painful. PL/I asked: *Why not give every programmer both—and allow structures of arrays and arrays of structures?*

questions.prompt: How does a record 'structure' differ fundamentally from a mathematical 'array'?
choices: An array holds a grid of elements of the same data type, whereas a structure groups named fields of different data types.
An array can only be one-dimensional, whereas a structure must always have at least three dimensions.
An array stores only character strings, whereas a structure stores only binary floating-point numbers.
An array is allocated in magnetic-core memory, whereas a structure can only exist on external magnetic tape.
questions.explanation: An array is a homogeneous collection (every element shares the same data attributes, accessed by numeric subscripts), whereas a structure is a heterogeneous collection grouping named fields of mixed types (text, integers, decimal currency) into a single logical record.

questions.prompt: Why was FORTRAN's array-only container model awkward for commercial customer files in 1960?
choices: FORTRAN arrays were limited by compiler rules to a maximum of ten elements per program.
A customer record mixes text names, dates, and decimal dollar balances, which do not share a single uniform numeric type.
Customer files required complex numbers with imaginary components that FORTRAN arrays could not store.
FORTRAN arrays could not be read from punch cards or written to line printers.
questions.explanation: Because all elements in a single FORTRAN array had to share one uniform data type, grouping mixed commercial fields (strings, dates, currency) into a single unit was unnatural in early FORTRAN.

chunks.title: Filing Cabinets in Code: Level-Numbered Hierarchical Structures
chunks.content_markdown:
To group mixed data into a neat tree of folders and sub-folders, PL/I adapted COBOL's **hierarchical structure**, using **level numbers** (`1`, `2`, `3`, ...) inside a `DECLARE` statement:

`DECLARE 1 CUSTOMER,`
`          2 NAME,`
`            3 FIRST CHAR(15),`
`            3 LAST  CHAR(20),`
`          2 BALANCE FIXED DEC(9,2);`

Think of level `1` (`CUSTOMER`) as the outer manila folder. Inside it sit two level-`2` items: a sub-folder called `NAME` (which itself contains two level-`3` text slips, `FIRST` and `LAST`) and a single currency number called `BALANCE`.

You can refer to an individual slip using a dot (**qualified name**), such as `CUSTOMER.NAME.LAST` (or simply `LAST` if no other structure in scope has a `LAST`). Even better, if you declare a second identical folder `BACKUP_CUST`, you can copy every single sub-folder and field in one stroke by writing `BACKUP_CUST = CUSTOMER;`!

questions.prompt: In a PL/I structure declaration like `DECLARE 1 EMP, 2 PAY, 3 SALARY FIXED DEC(8,2), 3 BONUS FIXED DEC(7,2);`, what do the numbers `1`, `2`, and `3` indicate?
choices: They specify how many array copies of each variable should be allocated in memory.
They specify the exact punch-card column numbers where each field must be punched.
They specify the nesting hierarchy from top-level record `EMP` down to sub-group `PAY` and leaf fields `SALARY` and `BONUS`.
They initialize the numeric values of `EMP`, `PAY`, and `SALARY` to 1, 2, and 3 at startup.
questions.explanation: Level numbers in a PL/I `DECLARE` statement define the tree-like containment hierarchy of a composite record structure, from the level-1 root container down to the elementary leaf fields.

questions.prompt: How does a PL/I programmer reference the `LAST` field specifically inside the `CUSTOMER` structure when another structure in the program also has a field named `LAST`?
choices: By enclosing the field name in parentheses after the level number, such as `3(LAST)`.
By joining the names with a hyphen, such as `CUSTOMER-NAME-LAST`.
By prefixing the field name with a percent sign, such as `%CUSTOMER_LAST`.
By writing a dot-qualified name such as `CUSTOMER.NAME.LAST` or `CUSTOMER.LAST`.
questions.explanation: PL/I uses dot qualification (`CUSTOMER.NAME.LAST`, or partial qualification `CUSTOMER.LAST` so long as it is unambiguous) to identify a specific field within a hierarchical structure.

chunks.title: Whole-Array Math and Asterisk Cross-Section Slicing
chunks.content_markdown:
While business programmers cheered for hierarchical structures, scientific programmers were dazzled by what PL/I could do with **arrays**. In FORTRAN, if you had two 100-element arrays `B` and `C` and wanted to add them together into array `A` (or set every element of `A` to zero), you had to write an explicit loop stepping through index `1` to `100`.

In PL/I, you can write **whole-array expressions** without a single loop keyword:

`A = 0;` *(sets every element of array `A` to zero!)*
`A = B + C;` *(adds every corresponding element of `B` and `C` into `A`!)*

What if you have a two-dimensional table `SALES(12, 5)`—12 months by 5 regions—and want to zero out *only Region 3 across all 12 months*, or copy *only Month 6 across all 5 regions*? PL/I introduced **asterisk cross-section slicing**: replacing a subscript with `*` selects that entire row or column:

`SALES(*, 3) = 0;` *(zeros out all 12 months of column 3!)*

questions.prompt: If `A`, `B`, and `C` are declared as 50-element numeric arrays in PL/I, what does the single statement `A = B + C;` accomplish?
choices: It adds each element of `B` to the corresponding element of `C` and stores all 50 sums into `A`.
It adds only the first elements `B(1)` and `C(1)` together and leaves the rest of `A` unchanged.
It concatenates `B` and `C` end-to-end to turn `A` into a 100-element array.
It triggers a compile-time error because PL/I arrays cannot be used without explicit subscripts.
questions.explanation: PL/I supports whole-array operations: writing `A = B + C;` automatically loops over all matching indices and performs element-by-element addition.

questions.prompt: Given a two-dimensional PL/I array `GRID(10, 20)` (10 rows by 20 columns), what does the cross-section expression `GRID(4, *)` represent?
choices: The single element at row 4, column 4, multiplied by all 20 columns.
The entire 4th row of `GRID` across all 20 columns, treated as a one-dimensional slice.
The first 4 rows of `GRID` summed together into a single scalar number.
The entire 4th column of `GRID` across all 10 rows, treated as a vertical slice.
questions.explanation: An asterisk (`*`) in a subscript position specifies an array cross-section across every index in that dimension, so `GRID(4, *)` selects all 20 columns of row 4.

chunks.title: Strings That Grow and Shrink: `VARYING` Character and Bit Strings
chunks.content_markdown:
Early FORTRAN barely acknowledged text at all, and COBOL forced every text field to have a rigid, fixed character length—so storing `'JOE'` inside a 25-character name field padded it with 22 trailing blank spaces.

PL/I treated text as a first-class citizen by offering both fixed-length `CHARACTER(n)` strings and flexible **`CHARACTER(n) VARYING`** strings:

`DECLARE CITY CHAR(30) VARYING;`

When you assign `CITY = 'BOSTON';`, the string's current length is genuinely `6` (up to its maximum capacity of `30`), tracked automatically by a hidden 2-byte length prefix in memory! Joining two strings together (**concatenation**) uses the double vertical bar operator (`||`), so `'NEW ' || 'YORK'` produces `'NEW YORK'` without 20 unwanted spaces in the middle.

And right beside `CHARACTER` strings, PL/I added **`BIT(n)`** strings—sequences of raw `0` and `1` bits like `'10110'B` that let systems programmers and commercial coders pack compact true/false status flags into a single byte.

questions.prompt: How does a `CHARACTER(30) VARYING` variable in PL/I behave differently from a fixed-length `CHARACTER(30)` variable when assigned the 4-letter string `'ROME'`?
choices: The `VARYING` variable repeats `'ROME'` to fill 30 characters, whereas the fixed-length variable stores only 4 characters.
The `VARYING` variable pads `'ROME'` with 26 leading zeros, whereas the fixed-length variable pads with 26 trailing spaces.
The `VARYING` variable tracks a current active length of 4, whereas the fixed-length variable pads `'ROME'` with 26 trailing spaces.
The `VARYING` variable permanently shrinks its maximum capacity to 4, whereas the fixed-length variable stays at 30.
questions.explanation: A fixed-length `CHAR(30)` variable is always 30 characters long (padding shorter strings on the right with blanks), whereas `CHAR(30) VARYING` tracks its actual current length dynamically from 0 up to 30.

questions.prompt: What are `BIT` strings (such as `DECLARE FLAGS BIT(8);`) used for in PL/I?
choices: Formatting currency numbers with automatic commas and suppressed leading zeros.
Storing base-10 packed decimal currency figures with two digits per byte.
Representing complex numbers with separate real and imaginary floating-point parts.
Storing and manipulating sequences of binary `0` and `1` values, such as compact true/false status flags.
questions.explanation: PL/I's `BIT` data type represents strings of binary digits (`'0'B` and `'1'B`) and supports boolean operations (`&` for AND, `|` for OR, `~` for NOT), making it ideal for boolean variables and compact hardware or account status flags.

chunks.title: Built-In String Slicing: The Versatile `SUBSTR` Function
chunks.content_markdown:
To make working with text and bit strings effortless, PL/I included a Swiss-Army-knife built-in function called **`SUBSTR`** (short for *substring*). Give `SUBSTR(string, start, length)` a string, a starting character position, and a length, and it extracts that exact piece of text:

`AREA_CODE = SUBSTR(PHONE_NUM, 1, 3);` *(pulls out the first 3 characters)*

Here comes a quintessential PL/I twist: `SUBSTR` can *also* sit on the **left-hand side** of an equals sign! In PL/I, a function used on the left side of `=` to modify a target is called a **pseudo-variable**. If `PHONE_NUM` currently holds `'212-555-0199'` and you write:

`SUBSTR(PHONE_NUM, 1, 3) = '415';`

PL/I surgically overwrites just characters 1 through 3 in place, turning `PHONE_NUM` into `'415-555-0199'` without disturbing the rest of the string!

Now that we have rich numbers, structures, arrays, and strings, where do all these containers live inside the computer's precious magnetic-core memory? In Section 8, we will meet PL/I's four storage classes.

questions.prompt: If the PL/I variable `CODE` holds the string `'ABCDEFGH'`, what value is returned by the expression `SUBSTR(CODE, 3, 4)`?
choices: `'CDEF'`, starting at the 3rd character and extracting 4 characters.
`'CD'`, extracting the characters from position 3 through position 4.
`'ABCD'`, taking the first 4 characters and shifting them 3 places.
`'DEFG'`, skipping the first 3 characters and extracting the next 4.
questions.explanation: `SUBSTR(string, start, length)` begins at 1-based position `start` (character 3, `'C'`) and extracts `length` characters (4 characters: `'CDEF'`).

questions.prompt: What happens in PL/I when `SUBSTR` is used as a 'pseudo-variable' on the left-hand side of an assignment, such as `SUBSTR(WORD, 2, 2) = 'XY';`?
choices: It triggers a syntax error because function names cannot appear to the left of an equals sign.
It replaces characters 2 and 3 of `WORD` in place with `'XY'`, leaving all other characters of `WORD` unchanged.
It inserts `'XY'` before character 2 and lengthens `WORD` by two characters.
It redefines the built-in `SUBSTR` function so it always returns `'XY'` for the rest of the block.
questions.explanation: As a PL/I pseudo-variable, `SUBSTR(WORD, 2, 2)` on the left side of `=` designates a target slice—starting at character 2 for length 2—to be overwritten in place.

sections.title: 8. Mastering Memory: STATIC, AUTOMATIC, CONTROLLED, and BASED Pointer Storage
sections.summary: Examine how PL/I gave mainstream programmers unprecedented control over scarce 1960s computer memory through four distinct storage classes. Beyond permanent `STATIC` variables (like FORTRAN) and `AUTOMATIC` variables created and erased as blocks started and finished (like ALGOL), PL/I introduced `CONTROLLED` push-down storage and `BASED` variables paired with `POINTER` addresses—bringing dynamic memory allocation (`ALLOCATE` and `FREE`) and linked-list data structures into everyday commercial and scientific programming.
introduced_terms: CONTROLLED storage (explicit ALLOCATE and FREE stacks)
BASED storage and POINTER variables (dynamic memory addressing)

chunks.title: Why 64 Kilobytes Forced Programmers to Care About Memory Lifetimes
chunks.content_markdown:
Today, even a cheap wristwatch has millions of bytes of memory. In 1965, however, main memory was built from tiny iron doughnuts called **magnetic cores** woven by hand onto grids of fine copper wire. A mid-sized IBM System/360 might have only **64 kilobytes** (65,536 bytes) of core memory to hold the operating system, the running program, and all of its data combined!

In FORTRAN and COBOL, every single variable and array in your program was **permanently reserved** in memory from the moment the program started until the moment it finished. If Subroutine A needed a 20,000-byte array only during the first ten seconds of a job, and Subroutine B needed a different 20,000-byte array during the last ten seconds, both arrays sat hogging 40,000 bytes for the entire run.

To break this bottleneck, PL/I gave programmers four distinct **storage classes** that controlled *when* a variable claimed memory and *when* it gave that memory back.

questions.prompt: Why was memory management such an urgent practical concern on mid-1960s IBM System/360 mainframes?
choices: Magnetic-core memory was hand-wired and expensive, so an entire machine often had only 32 to 256 kilobytes of main memory.
System/360 processors could only address a hardware maximum of 1,024 bytes of memory regardless of budget.
Magnetic-core memory lost its contents whenever a procedure returned, requiring data to be re-read from punch cards.
The operating system prohibited any single program from declaring more than twelve variables at a time.
questions.explanation: 1960s magnetic-core memory was physically bulky and costly, meaning mainframes often operated with only tens of kilobytes of core memory and needed ways to reuse memory across different phases of a program.

questions.prompt: How did traditional 1960s FORTRAN and COBOL allocate memory for variables and arrays during a program run?
choices: Every variable was allocated on a dynamic push-down stack when a subroutine started and freed when it returned.
Every variable occupied a permanent, fixed slot in memory from the start of the job until the entire program finished.
Every variable required an explicit `ALLOCATE` statement before its first use and a `FREE` statement afterward.
Variables were kept on external magnetic tape and never held in central magnetic-core memory.
questions.explanation: Both FORTRAN and COBOL used static allocation by default, keeping memory reserved for every variable throughout the entire run even when a subroutine was inactive.

chunks.title: `STATIC` vs. `AUTOMATIC`: Permanent Desks vs. Hotel Rooms
chunks.content_markdown:
PL/I's first two storage classes correspond to the difference between owning a permanent office desk and checking into a hotel room for the night:

1. **`STATIC` storage**: If you write `DECLARE COUNT FIXED BIN STATIC INIT(0);`, PL/I reserves a permanent memory slot before the program starts. Just like a permanent office desk, `COUNT` stays in place for the whole run; if a procedure adds `1` to `COUNT` and exits, that new value is still sitting on the desk the next time the procedure is called.
2. **`AUTOMATIC` storage (the PL/I default!)**: If you don't specify a storage class, local variables are `AUTOMATIC`. Like checking into a hotel room, PL/I allocates memory for `AUTOMATIC` variables on a hardware **stack** the instant your program enters their `PROCEDURE` or `BEGIN` block, and **automatically frees that memory** the instant the block ends!

Thanks to `AUTOMATIC` storage, ten big procedures that run one after another can share and recycle the exact same pool of scarce memory.

questions.prompt: What is the default storage class for ordinary local variables declared inside a PL/I `PROCEDURE` or `BEGIN` block?
choices: `STATIC`, meaning memory is reserved permanently before the program starts and kept until termination.
`CONTROLLED`, meaning memory is allocated only when the programmer executes an explicit `ALLOCATE` statement.
`AUTOMATIC`, meaning memory is allocated when the block is entered and automatically released when the block exits.
`BASED`, meaning the variable holds no memory of its own until aimed at an address by a pointer.
questions.explanation: In PL/I, local variables default to `AUTOMATIC`, meaning they are allocated dynamically on the runtime stack upon block entry and freed upon block exit.

questions.prompt: When should a PL/I programmer explicitly declare a local variable inside a procedure as `STATIC` rather than leaving it `AUTOMATIC`?
choices: When the procedure is `RECURSIVE` and needs a separate copy of the variable for each active call.
When the variable holds an array whose dimensions change dynamically on every entry to the block.
When the programmer wants the variable's memory to be reclaimed immediately upon leaving the procedure.
When the procedure needs the variable to remember its stored value from one call to the next.
questions.explanation: Because `AUTOMATIC` variables are created fresh on block entry and destroyed on exit, a variable that must retain its value across separate calls to a procedure (like a call counter) must be declared `STATIC`.

chunks.title: Taking the Steering Wheel: `CONTROLLED` Storage
chunks.content_markdown:
What if entering and leaving a block isn't flexible enough? Suppose you don't even know whether you'll need a giant 5,000-element table—or how big it should be—until halfway through reading a customer tape, and you want it to survive even after the current subroutine finishes.

For that, PL/I created **`CONTROLLED`** storage:

`DECLARE MATRIX(N, N) FLOAT BIN CONTROLLED;`

Simply declaring a `CONTROLLED` variable reserves **zero memory** at first. Instead, *you* take the steering wheel using two explicit commands:
- **`ALLOCATE MATRIX;`** grabs a fresh block of memory right then and there (using the current value of `N`!).
- **`FREE MATRIX;`** hands that memory right back to the system whenever you are done with it.

Here's a neat twist: if you run `ALLOCATE MATRIX;` a *second* time without freeing the first one, PL/I doesn't lose the first copy—it pushes the old `MATRIX` down onto a hidden stack! When you later say `FREE MATRIX;`, the top copy disappears and the previous generation pops right back into view.

questions.prompt: How does a PL/I programmer create and release memory for a variable declared with the `CONTROLLED` storage class?
choices: By executing explicit `ALLOCATE` and `FREE` statements at any desired point during the program's execution.
By entering and exiting a `BEGIN...END` block, which automatically allocates and frees `CONTROLLED` variables.
By setting a `POINTER` variable to zero when the memory is no longer needed.
By enabling the `(STORAGE):` condition prefix at the top of the main procedure.
questions.explanation: `CONTROLLED` variables exist only when explicitly allocated by an `ALLOCATE` statement and remain alive across block boundaries until explicitly released by a `FREE` statement.

questions.prompt: What happens in PL/I if a program executes `ALLOCATE X;` twice in a row for a `CONTROLLED` variable `X` without an intervening `FREE X;`?
choices: The program aborts immediately with a duplicate-allocation runtime condition.
PL/I stacks the allocations: the new copy of `X` becomes active on top, and a later `FREE X;` uncovers the earlier copy.
The first copy of `X` is permanently overwritten and its previous values are lost.
The second `ALLOCATE X;` statement is ignored and `X` keeps its original values.
questions.explanation: `CONTROLLED` storage acts as a push-down stack of generations for that variable name: each `ALLOCATE` pushes a new instance on top, and each `FREE` pops the most recent instance off, restoring the prior one.

chunks.title: Bringing Pointers to the Mainstream: `BASED` Storage and `POINTER` Variables
chunks.content_markdown:
What if you want to build a chain of fifty customer orders in memory—a **linked list** or a family tree—where you can jump directly to *any* item in the chain at any time, not just the top item of a stack?

To make that possible, PL/I introduced **`BASED`** storage paired with **`POINTER`** variables—one of the earliest and most influential appearances of explicit memory pointers in any mainstream high-level language!

A **`POINTER`** variable (`DECLARE P POINTER;`) does not hold a number or a name; it holds a **memory address**—an electronic street address pointing to a location in RAM. A **`BASED`** declaration (`DECLARE 1 NODE BASED(P), 2 VAL FIXED BIN, 2 NEXT POINTER;`) acts like a transparent stencil or template. Wherever pointer `P` is aimed, `NODE` lets you read or write the fields at that address—or use the arrow operator **`P -> VAL`** (`P` points to `VAL`) to inspect any node in a dynamic chain!

questions.prompt: What does a `POINTER` variable store in PL/I?
choices: The character name of a external magnetic tape file on the System/360.
The integer subscript index of an element inside a one-dimensional FORTRAN array.
The memory address (location) of a data item or dynamically allocated structure in memory.
The number of decimal digits to the right of the radix point in a `FIXED DECIMAL` variable.
questions.explanation: A `POINTER` (`PTR`) variable holds a machine memory address that can aim at any dynamically allocated `BASED` variable or existing data item (via the `ADDR` built-in function).

questions.prompt: In the PL/I expression `HEAD_PTR -> ORDER_TOTAL`, what does the arrow operator (`->`) mean?
choices: Subtract `ORDER_TOTAL` from `HEAD_PTR` and test whether the difference is positive.
Copy the value of `HEAD_PTR` into `ORDER_TOTAL` and reset `HEAD_PTR` to zero.
Convert `HEAD_PTR` from binary floating-point into the `PICTURE` format of `ORDER_TOTAL`.
Follow the memory address stored in `HEAD_PTR` to access the `ORDER_TOTAL` field of the `BASED` structure located there.
questions.explanation: PL/I's locator-qualification arrow (`->`) dereferences the pointer on the left (`HEAD_PTR`) to overlay and access the `BASED` variable or structure field on the right (`ORDER_TOTAL`)—syntax that directly inspired C's `->` operator.

chunks.title: Great Power, New Responsibility: The Four Storage Classes Together
chunks.content_markdown:
Look at the spectrum of memory tools PL/I handed to 1960s programmers:

- **`STATIC`**: Permanent memory for the whole program run (FORTRAN's world).
- **`AUTOMATIC`**: Stack memory created and freed automatically with every block entry and exit (ALGOL's world).
- **`CONTROLLED`**: Programmer-managed push-down stacks using `ALLOCATE` and `FREE`.
- **`BASED` + `POINTER`**: True dynamic heap structures (linked lists, trees, and zero-copy buffer overlays using `READ ... SET(P);`) navigated with `->` arrows.

Notice the double-edged sword of `BASED` pointers: if you point `P` at an area of memory that you already freed (a **dangling pointer**) or set `P = ADDR(X)` and overlay the wrong data template on top of `X`, the compiler cannot stop you from reading gibberish! What happens when a running program *does* hit an unexpected crisis—like dividing by zero or reaching the end of a tape? In Section 9, we will meet PL/I's runtime safety net.

questions.prompt: Which of PL/I's four storage classes is best suited for building a dynamic tree or linked list where nodes are connected by memory addresses?
choices: `BASED` storage paired with `POINTER` variables and the `->` locator operator.
`STATIC` storage paired with fixed-size integer arrays declared in the main procedure.
`AUTOMATIC` storage without any pointer variables or `ALLOCATE` statements.
`CONTROLLED` storage using implicit `I`–`N` first-letter variable typing.
questions.explanation: `BASED` structures allocated dynamically (`ALLOCATE NODE SET(P);`) and linked via `POINTER` fields (`P -> NEXT`) allow programmers to construct arbitrary linked lists, trees, and graphs.

questions.prompt: What risk accompanies the flexibility of `BASED` storage and `POINTER` variables if a programmer makes a mistake?
choices: Declaring a `POINTER` variable disables all `FIXED DECIMAL` arithmetic inside the same procedure.
A pointer aimed at freed memory or the wrong data type can read or overwrite unintended memory locations.
Pointers can only address the first 64 bytes of a structure and truncate any remaining fields.
Using the `->` operator automatically forces all local variables in the program to become `STATIC`.
questions.explanation: Because a `POINTER` in PL/I is an untyped machine address that can be aimed at any `BASED` template or freed memory block, careless pointer manipulation can cause dangling-pointer bugs or memory corruption.

sections.title: 9. Runtime Resilience: Asynchronous ON-Conditions and Early TASK/EVENT Multitasking
sections.summary: Learn how PL/I kept long-running mainframe jobs from crashing outright when unexpected trouble struck at 2:00 a.m. Using `ON` condition handlers (`ON ZERODIVIDE`, `ON OVERFLOW`, `ON ENDFILE`), a program could register standing emergency instructions that woke up automatically whenever hardware or input/output faults occurred, logged or repaired the problem, and kept running. PL/I also pioneered built-in `TASK` and `EVENT` keywords so a single program could launch concurrent background operations and synchronize with their completion.
introduced_terms: hardware and I/O interrupts (ZERODIVIDE, OVERFLOW, and ENDFILE)
TASK and EVENT multitasking (concurrent procedure execution)

chunks.title: The 2:00 A.M. Payroll Crash
chunks.content_markdown:
Picture an overnight batch run at a giant insurance company in 1963. For four hours, the mainframe has been humming through 200,000 policyholder records on magnetic tape. At 2:14 a.m., on record #189,402, a clerk's keypunch typo has left a policy's `MONTHS_ACTIVE` field as `0`. The program tries to calculate an average monthly claim by dividing by `MONTHS_ACTIVE`—**dividing by zero**!

In a standard 1960s FORTRAN program, the hardware arithmetic circuit immediately triggers a fatal fault, the operating system aborts the entire job, and the printer spits out fifty pages of cryptic raw memory numbers (a **memory dump**). The night shift is ruined.

Of course, the programmer *could* write an `IF MONTHS_ACTIVE = 0` check before every single division sign in a 10,000-line program, cluttering the business logic endlessly. The 3x3 Committee asked: *What if you could post a standing fire-drill rule once at the top of a block, and let the hardware wake it up only if an emergency actually strikes?*

questions.prompt: What typically happened in an early-1960s mainframe batch job when a program encountered an unexpected hardware fault like dividing by zero?
choices: The operating system immediately terminated the entire job and printed a raw memory dump.
The processor automatically substituted zero for the quotient and continued without warning.
The card reader paused the current record and skipped ahead to the next procedure block.
The compiler rewrote the division statement at runtime to divide by one instead of zero.
questions.explanation: Without built-in exception handling, an unhandled hardware interrupt like division by zero caused the operating system to abort the batch job and print a diagnostic storage dump.

questions.prompt: Why was placing manual `IF` tests before every single arithmetic operation an unsatisfying way to guard against runtime faults?
choices: PL/I allowed at most three `IF` statements inside any single `PROCEDURE` block.
It cluttered the program's main logic with repetitive error checks and still could not catch every hardware overflow or I/O fault.
Using an `IF` statement before division automatically converted `FIXED DECIMAL` numbers into `FLOAT BINARY`.
Manual `IF` statements could only test character strings and could not compare numeric variables to zero.
questions.explanation: Scattering manual `IF` checks before every division, multiplication, or input statement buried the real algorithm under defensive boilerplate and still could not easily intercept intermediate arithmetic overflows.

chunks.title: Standing Fire Drills: The `ON` Statement and `ON`-Units
chunks.content_markdown:
PL/I solved the 2:00 a.m. crash by inventing structured **exception handling** through the **`ON` statement**—the direct ancestor of `EXCEPTION WHEN` in Ada and SQL and `try / catch` in modern languages like Java, C++, and Python!

At the start of a block, a programmer registers a standing emergency rule:

`ON ZERODIVIDE BEGIN;`
`   PUT SKIP LIST('BAD ZERO DIVISOR IN RECORD:', CUST_ID);`
`   AVG_CLAIM = 0;`
`   GO TO NEXT_RECORD;`
`END;`

Let's unpack the two parts of this statement:
- **`ZERODIVIDE`** is the **ON-condition**: the named emergency event you are watching for.
- The `BEGIN ... END;` block (or single statement) is the **ON-unit**: a small standby handler that **does not run right now** when the `ON` statement is passed! Instead, it waits quietly in the background. If a division by zero happens *anywhere* inside that procedure—or even inside a deeply nested subroutine it calls—the hardware interrupt immediately triggers your `ON`-unit!

questions.prompt: When a PL/I program executes the statement `ON ZERODIVIDE CALL LOG_ERROR;`, when does `CALL LOG_ERROR;` actually run?
choices: Immediately at the moment the `ON` statement is reached, before any division is attempted.
Once at the very end of the procedure block as part of normal cleanup.
Only if and when a division by zero actually occurs while that `ON` handler is active.
During the compile-time preprocessor pass before machine code is generated.
questions.explanation: Executing an `ON` statement does not run its attached `ON`-unit right away; it establishes a dynamic handler that triggers asynchronously if the named condition is raised later during execution.

questions.prompt: What happens if Procedure A establishes an `ON ZERODIVIDE` handler and then calls Subroutine B, which divides by zero without having its own handler?
choices: Subroutine B aborts the job because `ON` handlers cannot apply across `CALL` boundaries.
The compiler refuses to compile Subroutine B unless it repeats the exact same `ON` statement.
The division by zero is ignored and Subroutine B returns an uninitialized pointer.
PL/I searches backward through the active call chain and invokes Procedure A's `ON ZERODIVIDE` handler.
questions.explanation: PL/I `ON`-units are dynamically scoped along the call stack: if a called subroutine raises a condition it does not handle locally, PL/I unwinds up the active call chain to find the most recently established handler.

chunks.title: A Whole Catalog of Conditions: Hardware, Files, and Custom Signals
chunks.content_markdown:
PL/I didn't stop at division by zero. It gave programmers a comprehensive catalog of built-in **ON-conditions** covering nearly everything that could happen inside a computer:

- **Arithmetic hardware interrupts**: `ZERODIVIDE`, `OVERFLOW` (a floating-point number grew larger than the hardware exponent limit), `UNDERFLOW` (a number shrank too close to zero), and `FIXEDOVERFLOW` (a fixed-point sum overflowed its declared digit count).
- **Input/Output events**: `ENDFILE(TAPE1)` (reached the end of a magnetic tape or card deck—turning normal end-of-file loop termination into a clean event!), `TRANSMIT` (a damaged spot on a magnetic tape caused a corrupted-character read error), and `ENDPAGE(PRT)` (the line printer reached the bottom margin of a paper sheet, so your `ON ENDPAGE` handler could automatically print a fresh page header and page number!).
- **Debugging and custom conditions**: Programmers could even invent their own named condition (`ON CONDITION(BAD_AUDIT) ...`) and trigger it deliberately from anywhere using **`SIGNAL CONDITION(BAD_AUDIT);`**!

questions.prompt: How did business programmers commonly use the `ON ENDPAGE(PRINTER)` condition in PL/I report programs?
choices: To automatically print a page title, column headings, and an incremented page number whenever a report filled a sheet of paper.
To close all magnetic tape files and terminate the program as soon as the first page finished printing.
To detect when a punch-card reader hopper ran out of input cards during a batch job.
To suppress leading zeros inside `PICTURE` currency fields on the final line of a ledger.
questions.explanation: Whenever output reached the bottom line of a page, PL/I automatically raised `ENDPAGE`, allowing an `ON ENDPAGE` handler to start a new page with formatted headers and return smoothly to wherever printing had paused.

questions.prompt: Which PL/I statement lets a programmer intentionally trigger an `ON`-condition (either built-in or user-defined) for testing or custom error handling?
choices: `ALLOCATE` (for example, `ALLOCATE ZERODIVIDE;`).
`SIGNAL` (for example, `SIGNAL ZERODIVIDE;` or `SIGNAL CONDITION(BAD_AUDIT);`).
`RETURN` (for example, `RETURN CONDITION(BAD_AUDIT);`).
`DECLARE` (for example, `DECLARE ZERODIVIDE AUTOMATIC;`).
questions.explanation: The `SIGNAL` statement raises a specified condition in software just as if the condition had occurred naturally, firing whatever `ON`-unit is currently established for it.

chunks.title: Checking Whether Arrays Stay in Bounds: Condition Prefixes
chunks.content_markdown:
What about bugs that hardware doesn't catch automatically—like an array declared with 10 slots (`DECLARE SCORES(10);`) where a buggy loop tries to write into slot `SCORES(11)`? In FORTRAN, writing past the end of an array silently clobbered whatever poor variable happened to sit next in memory!

PL/I introduced the **`SUBSCRIPTRANGE`** condition (abbreviated `SUBRG`) to catch out-of-bounds array subscripts red-handed, along with **`STRINGRANGE`** (for bad `SUBSTR` positions) and **`SIZE`** (when assigning a big number into a smaller variable chops off high-order digits).

Because checking every single array subscript takes extra processor cycles, PL/I let programmers switch individual checks **on or off** for any block or statement using a parenthesized **condition prefix** before a colon:

`(SUBSCRIPTRANGE): CALC: PROCEDURE;`

During testing, you turned `(SUBSCRIPTRANGE):` on to catch every stray subscript; once debugged, you could turn `(NOSUBSCRIPTRANGE):` off in inner loops for maximum speed!

questions.prompt: What bug does enabling the `(SUBSCRIPTRANGE):` condition prefix on a PL/I procedure catch at runtime?
choices: Any attempt to use a PL/I command keyword like `IF` or `DO` as an array name.
Any attempt to type an array declaration past column 72 on an 80-column card.
Any attempt to read or write an array element using an index outside the array's declared lower and upper bounds.
Any attempt to allocate a `CONTROLLED` array more than once without freeing it first.
questions.explanation: When `SUBSCRIPTRANGE` is enabled, the compiler inserts runtime bounds checks on array references and raises the `SUBSCRIPTRANGE` condition if an index falls outside the declared bounds.

questions.prompt: Why did PL/I allow programmers to enable or disable conditions like `(SUBSCRIPTRANGE):` and `(NOSUBSCRIPTRANGE):` on specific blocks?
choices: Because enabling `SUBSCRIPTRANGE` disabled all `ON ZERODIVIDE` and `ON ENDFILE` handlers in that block.
Because the System/360 hardware could only check bounds on one-dimensional arrays, not two-dimensional grids.
Because `SUBSCRIPTRANGE` was only legal inside `BEGIN...END` blocks and forbidden on `PROCEDURE` blocks.
So programmers could enable thorough safety checks while debugging and disable expensive checks in speed-critical production loops.
questions.explanation: Condition prefixes let programmers balance safety and performance: enabling `SUBSCRIPTRANGE` caught subtle memory-corrupting bugs during testing, while `NOSUBSCRIPTRANGE` avoided runtime checking overhead where speed was critical.

chunks.title: Ahead of Its Time: Built-In `TASK` and `EVENT` Multitasking
chunks.content_markdown:
Even while handling asynchronous faults, a single System/360 processor often spent precious milliseconds waiting for slow mechanical disk arms or tape drives to spin. Why let the fast electronic processor sit idle while a slow disk seeks?

Remarkably for 1964, PL/I built **concurrent multitasking** directly into the programming language itself—decades before mainstream languages like Java or C++ added built-in threads!

When calling a procedure in PL/I, you could attach **`TASK`** and **`EVENT`** options:

`CALL FETCH_RECORDS(TAPE_BUF) TASK(BG_WORKER) EVENT(DONE_FLAG);`

Instead of waiting for `FETCH_RECORDS` to finish, the main program **kept running immediately in parallel**, doing useful math while `BG_WORKER` ran concurrently under the System/360 operating system! Later, when the main program actually needed the fetched data, it executed **`WAIT(DONE_FLAG);`**, pausing only until the background task signaled completion. Next, in our final section, we will see how PL/I even let programs write *themselves* before compilation!

questions.prompt: What happens when a PL/I program calls a procedure with the `EVENT` option, such as `CALL UPDATE_LEDGER(ACCT) EVENT(E1);`?
choices: The procedure launches as a concurrent asynchronous task while the caller continues, synchronizing later via `WAIT(E1);`.
The procedure is registered as an inactive `ON`-unit that runs only if a hardware error occurs.
The procedure runs at compile time inside the macro preprocessor before machine code is generated.
The procedure executes ten times in a loop and stores the elapsed clock time in `E1`.
questions.explanation: Attaching `TASK` or `EVENT` to a `CALL` spawns concurrent execution of the called procedure, allowing the calling program to continue working in parallel until it synchronizes with `WAIT(event_variable);`.

questions.prompt: Why was built-in multitasking (`TASK`, `EVENT`, and `WAIT`) especially valuable on a 1960s mainframe?
choices: It eliminated the need to declare storage classes by making all variables `STATIC` automatically.
It allowed the fast central processor to keep performing calculations while another task waited for slow disk or tape I/O.
It allowed a program to bypass the operating system and control mechanical card readers without device drivers.
It doubled the precision of `FLOAT BINARY` variables from 27 bits to 54 bits during parallel calls.
questions.explanation: By overlapping compute-bound tasks with input/output-bound tasks, PL/I multitasking kept the expensive System/360 CPU busy instead of stalling every time a program waited on mechanical disk or tape drives.

sections.title: 10. The Compile-Time Macro Preprocessor and the 1966 Universal-Language Dream
sections.summary: Conclude Part I with PL/I's built-in compile-time macro preprocessor (`%DECLARE`, `%DO`, `%INCLUDE`), a 'program that writes the program' before normal compilation even begins, allowing shops to customize code automatically and share standard data definitions across teams. With the delivery of IBM's production F-level compiler in 1966, optimism reached a peak that PL/I would soon sweep away both FORTRAN and COBOL—setting the stage for Part II's look at compiler engineering hurdles, Multics systems programming, dialects, and PL/I's enduring legacy.

chunks.title: One Company, Forty-Eight Slightly Different Programs
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine a national retail chain in 1966 with branches in forty-eight states. Every state has the same basic payroll structure, so copying and maintaining forty-eight separate payroll programs is a nightmare. Worse still, twenty different programs at headquarters all read the exact same `CUSTOMER` master file; if someone adds a new `ZIP_CODE` field to that file, twenty programmers have to hand-edit twenty separate card decks without making a single typo!

How can one master program automatically tailor its own source code before the compiler even translates it? To solve this, PL/I built a powerful **compile-time macro preprocessor** right into the language.

Instead of inventing a cryptic, separate macro syntax, PL/I made an intuitive choice: **the preprocessor language is a miniature version of PL/I itself**, marked by a leading percent sign (**`%`**)!

questions.prompt: What is the role of PL/I's compile-time preprocessor before the main compiler translates a program into machine code?
choices: It scans the source text for `%` commands and automatically inserts, customizes, or generates PL/I source code.
It allocates `AUTOMATIC` stack frames in magnetic-core memory while the program is running at 2:00 a.m.
It sorts dropped paper punch cards by reading the sequence numbers in columns 73 through 80.
It converts `FLOAT BINARY` hardware registers into `FIXED DECIMAL` registers during execution.
questions.explanation: The compile-time preprocessor executes `%`-prefixed directives before main compilation begins, transforming and generating the PL/I source text that the compiler then translates into machine code.

questions.prompt: How does a programmer visually distinguish a compile-time preprocessor statement from an ordinary runtime PL/I statement?
choices: Preprocessor statements must be punched strictly in columns 1 through 6 of a card.
Preprocessor statements begin with a percent sign (`%`), such as `%DECLARE`, `%INCLUDE`, or `%DO`.
Preprocessor statements end with a colon (`:`) instead of a semicolon (`;`).
Preprocessor statements are enclosed inside `/*` and `*/` comment delimiters.
questions.explanation: PL/I uses a leading percent sign (`%`) to mark compile-time preprocessor statements (`%DECLARE`, `%INCLUDE`, `%IF`, `%DO`, `%PROCEDURE`), which use familiar PL/I syntax at compile time.

chunks.title: Single Source of Truth: `%INCLUDE` and `%DECLARE`
chunks.content_markdown:
The simplest and most beloved preprocessor command in corporate data centers was **`%INCLUDE`**. Instead of retyping the 50-line `DECLARE 1 CUSTOMER ...` structure into twenty different programs, the data administrator stored that structure once in a central disk library under the name `CUSTREC`. Then every programmer simply wrote one line:

`%INCLUDE CUSTREC;`

Before compilation began, the preprocessor fetched `CUSTREC` from the library and spliced those exact 50 lines right into the program! If `ZIP_CODE` was added later, updating `CUSTREC` once updated every recompiled program automatically.

Even better, using **`%DECLARE`** (or `%DCL`), a programmer could create compile-time variables that acted as find-and-replace templates across the entire program:

`%DECLARE MAX_ITEMS FIXED;`
`%MAX_ITEMS = 500;`
`DECLARE INVENTORY(MAX_ITEMS) FIXED DEC(7,2);`

Before the compiler saw the third line, the preprocessor replaced `MAX_ITEMS` with `500`, handing the compiler `DECLARE INVENTORY(500) FIXED DEC(7,2);`!

questions.prompt: How did the `%INCLUDE` directive improve software maintenance in large corporate data centers?
choices: It allowed programs to run without declaring variables by inferring all structure fields at runtime.
It automatically caught out-of-bounds array subscripts without needing `(SUBSCRIPTRANGE):`.
It let dozens of programs pull a shared record declaration from a single central library file, avoiding duplicate typing and mismatches.
It translated legacy COBOL source files into FORTRAN subroutines during magnetic tape reads.
questions.explanation: `%INCLUDE` spliced shared source text (such as standard file record layouts) from a central library into any program at compile time, ensuring every program used the exact same definition.

questions.prompt: If a PL/I program contains `%DCL TAX_COL CHAR; %TAX_COL = 'STATE_TAX';` followed by `TOTAL = PRICE + TAX_COL;`, what code does the main compiler actually see?
choices: `TOTAL = PRICE + 0;`, because character macro variables evaluate to zero in arithmetic formulas.
`TOTAL = PRICE + 'TAX_COL';`, with literal single quotes placed around the macro variable name.
A compile-time error, because `%DCL` variables can only substitute inside `DECLARE` statements.
`TOTAL = PRICE + STATE_TAX;`, because the preprocessor substitutes `STATE_TAX` for `TAX_COL` before compilation.
questions.explanation: A preprocessor `%DECLARE` variable replaces matching identifiers in the program text during the macro pass, so `TAX_COL` is substituted with `STATE_TAX` before the main compiler parses the statement.

chunks.title: A Program That Writes a Program: `%IF`, `%DO`, and `%PROCEDURE`
chunks.content_markdown:
Because PL/I's preprocessor included **`%IF ... %THEN ... %ELSE`**, **`%DO ... %END`**, and even compile-time functions (**`%PROCEDURE`**), a program could literally compute and write its own source code at compile time!

Suppose an aerospace engineer wants a super-fast sequence that adds three array elements without paying the runtime cost of incrementing and checking a loop counter (a technique called **loop unrolling**). Instead of typing repetitive lines by hand, the programmer writes a compile-time `%DO` loop:

`%DO I = 1 %TO 3;`
`   SUM = SUM + DATA(I);`
`%END;`

When the preprocessor runs, it executes that loop three times and emits three separate plain-text statements for the compiler:

`SUM = SUM + DATA(1);`
`SUM = SUM + DATA(2);`
`SUM = SUM + DATA(3);`

And with `%IF STATE = 'NY' %THEN ...`, one master deck could customize itself into lean, state-specific payroll programs with zero unused code left behind!

questions.prompt: What is produced when the PL/I preprocessor executes a compile-time `%DO I = 1 %TO 3; ... %END;` loop wrapping a statement?
choices: It generates three repeated copies of the statement in the source text with `I` replaced by 1, 2, and 3 before main compilation.
It spawns three concurrent `TASK` threads at runtime that execute the statement simultaneously.
It allocates three generations of a `CONTROLLED` variable on a push-down stack at runtime.
It restricts the loop so it can only execute during the first three seconds of a batch job.
questions.explanation: A compile-time `%DO` loop runs inside the preprocessor and stamps out repeated, customized lines of PL/I source text (unrolling the loop before the compiler translates the code).

questions.prompt: Why was using `%IF ... %THEN` at compile time more efficient for multi-state payroll customization than using ordinary runtime `IF ... THEN` statements?
choices: Ordinary runtime `IF` statements could not compare character strings like `'NY'` for equality.
Only the target state's code was compiled into the finished program, saving scarce System/360 memory and avoiding runtime checks.
Compile-time `%IF` statements automatically converted all binary variables into `FIXED DECIMAL`.
Runtime `IF` statements required reserved keywords, whereas `%IF` statements did not.
questions.explanation: Conditional compilation via `%IF` strips out irrelevant branches before compilation, keeping the final machine-code program compact in scarce 64 KB core memory and eliminating repeated runtime branch tests.

chunks.title: August 1966: The IBM F-Level Compiler Arrives
chunks.content_markdown:
Turning all ten sections of this grand vision into a working compiler on a 1960s mainframe was a heroic feat of software engineering. On System/360, IBM classified its software by memory tier using letter codes: **D-level** (16 KB min), **E-level** (32 KB), **F-level** (64 KB), and so on.

In **August 1966**, IBM's Hursley Laboratory in England delivered the landmark **PL/I (F) compiler** for OS/360. How on earth do you squeeze a compiler that understands context-sensitive unreserved keywords, floating-point and `FIXED DECIMAL` math, `PICTURE` masks, hierarchical structures, array cross-sections, `BASED` pointers, `ON`-conditions, multitasking, and a `%` macro preprocessor into **64 kilobytes of magnetic-core memory**?

The Hursley team designed PL/I (F) as a **multi-phase overlay compiler**: dozens of separate compiler phases lived on disk and swapped into memory one after another like relay runners passing a baton, gradually transforming PL/I source code into System/360 machine code!

questions.prompt: What did the letter 'F' signify in the name of IBM's landmark 1966 'PL/I (F)' production compiler?
choices: That the compiler was restricted to `FLOAT` scientific numbers and excluded `FIXED DECIMAL`.
That it was a preliminary field-test prototype rather than an official production release.
IBM's System/360 memory-size tier for machines with at least 64 kilobytes of main storage.
That the compiler translated FORTRAN source decks into PL/I source text.
questions.explanation: In IBM System/360 software nomenclature, letter codes indicated the minimum core memory partition required: D = 16 KB, E = 32 KB, F = 64 KB, G = 128 KB, and H = 256 KB.

questions.prompt: How did IBM's Hursley engineers fit a full-featured PL/I (F) compiler into a 64-kilobyte System/360 memory space?
choices: They dropped structures, pointers, and `ON`-conditions from the 1966 production release.
They required programmers to run the macro preprocessor on a separate IBM 1401 machine.
They limited user programs to a maximum of 100 lines of source code per compilation.
They structured the compiler as dozens of sequential phases on disk that loaded into memory one after another in overlays.
questions.explanation: Because the full compiler was far larger than 64 KB, PL/I (F) was engineered as tens of separate compilation phases that swapped in from disk storage in succession to analyze, optimize, and generate code.

chunks.title: The High-Water Mark of Universal-Language Optimism (and What Lies Ahead)
chunks.content_markdown:
When PL/I (F) shipped in late 1966, optimism across IBM, SHARE, and GUIDE reached a breathtaking high-water mark. Proponents of the **universal programming language paradigm** confidently predicted that within five years, both FORTRAN and COBOL would fade into history museums.

Look at everything we have traced across Part I:
- **The Problem (Sections 1–3)**: Two incompatible tribes—scientific FORTRAN (`FLOAT BINARY`) and commercial COBOL (`FIXED DECIMAL` and records)—united by IBM's System/360 and the 1963 3x3 Committee.
- **The Syntax & Data (Sections 4–7)**: Free-form `;` streams, `PROCEDURE`/`BEGIN` blocks, recursion, zero reserved keywords, unified numbers (`FLOAT BIN`, `FIXED DEC`, `PICTURE`), hierarchical structures, array `*` slices, and `VARYING` strings.
- **The Power Tools (Sections 8–10)**: Four storage classes (`STATIC`, `AUTOMATIC`, `CONTROLLED`, `BASED` pointers), asynchronous `ON`-conditions, `TASK`/`EVENT` multitasking, and the `%` compile-time preprocessor.

Why, then, didn't FORTRAN and COBOL surrender quietly after 1966—and how did PL/I go on to power the pioneering **Multics** operating system and shape C, Ada, and modern computing? That dramatic story awaits us in **Part II**!

questions.prompt: What was the core belief of the 'universal programming language paradigm' championed by PL/I advocates in 1966?
choices: A single richly featured language with sensible defaults could serve scientific, commercial, and systems programmers better than separate specialized languages.
Every computer manufacturer should hard-wire COBOL English sentences directly into processor silicon.
Programming languages should eliminate compilers and return to manual machine-code programming.
Scientific and commercial computing should remain permanently divided across separate hardware lines.
questions.explanation: PL/I embodied the universal language vision: that one coherent, modular language could unify scientific math, commercial data processing, and systems programming on unified hardware like the System/360.

questions.prompt: Which group of PL/I architectural milestones from Part I directly anticipated features that became standard in later languages like C, Ada, Java, and SQL?
choices: Mandatory column-7 card margins, 300 reserved English verbs, and static-only subroutine memory.
Free-form `/*...*/` comments and `;` syntax, block scope and recursion, `->` pointers, `ON`-condition exception handling, and `%` preprocessing.
Base-2-only currency rounding, un-nested global variables, and fixed-length-only character strings.
Implicit `I`–`N` variable typing, column-73 sequence numbers, and hardware word-mark bits.
questions.explanation: PL/I pioneered or popularized industrial use of `/* ... */` comments, semicolon-terminated block structure, `->` pointer qualification, asynchronous exception handling (`ON`), multitasking (`TASK`/`EVENT`), and compile-time preprocessing (`%`).
